# Postkit full documentation

Generated from the canonical Postkit guides and public package READMEs.

## Introduction

Source: /docs/introduction

Postkit is a portable publishing toolkit. It gives articles a shared component
vocabulary (callouts, figures, code blocks, link previews and more) and keeps
that vocabulary separate from the application that renders it. Write the
content once, then render it with Chakra UI, in an email, in Astro, or through
any framework adapter.

Postkit separates authored meaning from application infrastructure.

## The content contract

Components such as `Callout`, `Figure`, `Audio`, and `LinkPreview` describe
article intent. Their declarations define names, directive syntax, accepted
props, and whether they contain Markdown children.

The versioned `@postkit/core` document preserves semantic elements, rich
component names, literal props, and children independently of any renderer.
It can be parsed from or serialized to HTML, Markdown, safe literal MDX, and
JSON. The component contract can also be authored as JSX in trusted MDX or as
literal-only directives in plain Markdown.

The declaration manifest is the machine-readable form of that contract. It
describes each component, its plain-Markdown directive, child mode, and prop
schema, so editors and other authoring tools can use it without importing the
React renderer. The [component catalog](/components) is generated from the
same source.

## The renderer

Each environment maps the portable declaration to a real component. React's
`DocumentRenderer` maps semantic nodes and declarations to Chakra-backed
components. Astro bridges the same declarations into Astro components and
hydrates only the interactive parts. `@postkit/email` shares the portable
props where their meaning carries over and uses explicit fallbacks for
interactions that email clients do not support.

## The host application

The application owns:

- Page layout and navigation
- Routing policy
- Chakra tokens and site theme
- Media storage and URL generation
- Secrets and remote provider credentials
- Caching and persistence

Postkit provides explicit extension points for these responsibilities instead
of assuming one deployment architecture. Adapters do not configure the
application's content loader, authentication, asset storage, secrets,
deployment platform, or outer page layout.

## Choosing a package

Install the package closest to the application boundary. Framework adapters
use the Chakra-based React component system and add their native routing
behavior.

| Package                    | Choose it for                                                                          |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@postkit/core`            | Versioned HTML, Markdown, MDX, and JSON interchange without a React dependency         |
| `@postkit/react`           | `createPostkit`, kits, and headless React views you style yourself                     |
| `@postkit/chakra`          | React components, Chakra theming, Markdown directives, or a framework-neutral MDX map  |
| `@postkit/email`           | Chakra Email rendering with explicit email-safe component fallbacks                    |
| `@postkit/shiki`           | Lazy Shiki syntax highlighting for Postkit and Chakra code blocks                      |
| `@postkit/next`            | Next.js MDX and `next/link`                                                            |
| `@postkit/react-router`    | React Router and router-native internal links                                          |
| `@postkit/tanstack-router` | TanStack Router and application-defined typed route resolution                         |
| `@postkit/astro`           | Astro Markdown/MDX and selective React hydration                                       |
| `@postkit/unfurl`          | Server-side or build-time URL metadata normalization                                   |
| `@postkit/cli`             | The `postkit` command: turn on kits, eject and scaffold components, write the manifest |

Continue with [Installation](/docs/installation) for the install command that
matches your stack, or go straight to the [Quick start](/docs/quick-start).

## Installation

Source: /docs/installation

Postkit packages are ESM-only, publish TypeScript declarations, and emit
ES2022 JavaScript. The host application's framework and build tool must support
those package conventions.

## Install a renderer

Postkit has two React renderers. `@postkit/react` holds `createPostkit`, the
[kits](/docs/kits) and the headless views; `@postkit/chakra` adds the Chakra UI
views.

Most sites start with the [Chakra UI renderer](/docs/chakra) and its peer
dependencies:

```sh
npm install @postkit/react @postkit/chakra @chakra-ui/react @emotion/react react react-dom
```

For the [headless renderer](/docs/headless), which ships no styles and no
Chakra or Emotion, install `@postkit/react` and [Zag](https://zagjs.com), which
runs its interactive components:

```sh
npm install @postkit/react react react-dom
npm install @zag-js/react @zag-js/core @zag-js/types @zag-js/carousel @zag-js/tabs @zag-js/clipboard
```

The Zag packages are optional peer dependencies of `@postkit/react`, so a
Chakra site uses the copy Chakra already installs and never bundles Zag twice.

`@postkit/chakra` was named `@postkit/react` before 0.3.0. Coming from 0.2,
replace the dependency with `@postkit/chakra` and update your imports; the
component API is unchanged. From 0.3.0, `@postkit/react` is the headless
renderer.

## Add a framework adapter

Framework adapters add native routing around the same component map. Each
takes `@postkit/react` and `@postkit/chakra` as peer dependencies, and npm
installs them with it. Install the one that matches the application:

```sh
# Next.js
npm install @postkit/next @postkit/chakra

# React Router
npm install @postkit/react-router @postkit/chakra react-router

# TanStack Router
npm install @postkit/tanstack-router @postkit/chakra @tanstack/react-router

# Astro
npm install @postkit/astro @postkit/chakra
```

Each framework guide lists the remaining integration steps:
[Next.js](/docs/nextjs), [React Router](/docs/react-router),
[TanStack Router](/docs/tanstack-router), and [Astro](/docs/astro).

## Optional packages

An API, feed processor, or non-React content service can use the core document
contract by itself:

```sh
npm install @postkit/core
```

Add `@postkit/unfurl` to the server or build pipeline when the site renders link
previews:

```sh
npm install @postkit/unfurl
```

Add `@postkit/shiki` when rendered code blocks need syntax highlighting:

```sh
npm install @postkit/shiki
```

Add `@postkit/cli` as a dev dependency for the `postkit` command, which turns
on kits, ejects and scaffolds components, and writes the manifest (see
[CLI](/docs/cli)):

```sh
npm install --save-dev @postkit/cli
```

An HTML email build should use `@postkit/email` (see [Email](/docs/email))
rather than aliasing Chakra UI to an email primitive package. It shares portable Postkit props where the
meaning carries over and deliberately changes the output for interactions that
email clients do not support.

## Requirements

| Integration     | Supported range |
| --------------- | --------------- |
| React           | React 19        |
| Chakra UI       | `>=3.29.0 <4`   |
| Next.js         | `>=15 <17`      |
| React Router    | `>=7 <8`        |
| TanStack Router | `>=1.120 <2`    |
| Astro           | `>=6.4 <8`      |

The package manifests are authoritative for exact peer dependency ranges. Pin
related `@postkit/*` packages to the same release version. See
[Compatibility](/docs/compatibility) for the runtime matrix and hydration notes.

## Quick start

Source: /docs/quick-start

Postkit gives articles a portable component vocabulary while leaving the host
application in control of routing, layout, assets, and remote services. This
page uses the Chakra UI renderer (see [Installation](/docs/installation)); the
[headless renderer](#headless-instead) works the same way.

## Configure Postkit

Choose the [kits](/docs/kits) your writers need, and the renderer:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { chakra } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, media, technical } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article, technical, media],
});
```

[`createPostkit`](/docs/create-postkit) returns the provider, the MDX map, the
Remark plugins and the [manifest](/docs/manifest) for exactly that set.

## Render a first component

Mount the provider near the article:

```tsx
import { Callout } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { postkitDefaultTheme } from '@postkit/chakra/theme';

import { postkit } from './lib/postkit';

export function Article() {
  return (
    <postkit.Provider preset={postkitDefaultTheme}>
      <article>
        <h1>My first Postkit article</h1>
        <Callout title="Portable by default" tone="tip">
          Keep the content. Change the renderer.
        </Callout>
      </article>
    </postkit.Provider>
  );
}
```

With `renderer: chakra`, `postkit.Provider` is Chakra's `PostkitProvider`
with your site's defaults and overrides, and takes the same props.

The preset gives a standalone article Postkit's visual defaults. In an existing
Chakra application, omit `preset` and pass the site's system through `system`.
Postkit then uses the host's component recipes for headings, links, buttons,
inputs, tables, tabs, code, and other primitives. Add Postkit's preset only when
its content-specific visual defaults are wanted. [Tokens](/docs/tokens) explains
the layering.

## Add Markdown or MDX

Pass the component map and the Remark plugins to the application's Markdown or
MDX runtime:

```ts
import { postkit } from './lib/postkit';

export const mdxOptions = { remarkPlugins: postkit.remarkPlugins };
export const mdxComponents = postkit.mdxComponents;
```

The map holds only the components your kits enable, and the plugins
[validate](/docs/validation) directives and component names against the same
set, so a post that uses a component you didn't turn on fails the build.

Framework packages add native routing and framework-specific behavior around
this same map. `@postkit/next`, `@postkit/react-router` and
`@postkit/tanstack-router` each export a `createPostkit` that sets the
framework's link for you. Pick yours under Frameworks: [Next.js](/docs/nextjs),
[React Router](/docs/react-router), [TanStack Router](/docs/tanstack-router),
or [Astro](/docs/astro).

Write components as JSX in [MDX](/docs/mdx), or as literal-only
[Markdown directives](/docs/markdown-directives) in plain Markdown.

## Headless instead

To style the components yourself, with no Chakra or Emotion, leave out
`renderer`, and the views come from `@postkit/react`:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, media, technical } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, technical, media],
});
```

For a quiet starting look, import the optional baseline stylesheet once, at
your app's root:

```ts
import '@postkit/react/styles.css';
```

See [Headless](/docs/headless) for the install and styling.

## Keep sensitive work on the server

Link previews and social metadata can require network access or provider
credentials. Resolve them with `@postkit/unfurl` in a server or build-time
boundary, then pass normalized data to the renderer. See
[Link previews and unfurling](/docs/link-previews).

## Kits

Source: /docs/kits

A kit is a named set of component definitions. Postkit's 38 components come in
six kits, and you turn on the ones your writers use. Only those components are
bundled, validated and described in your manifest.

## The six kits

| Kit          | Import                           | Components                                                                                                       |
| ------------ | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `article`    | `@postkit/react/kits/article`    | Aside, AudienceBoundary, Callout, CardGrid, Disclosure, Footnote, Footnotes, KeyTakeaway, PullQuote, Steps, Tabs |
| `technical`  | `@postkit/react/kits/technical`  | Chart, CodeBlock, CodeGroup, Comparison, Diff, FileCard, FileTree, Stat, Terminal                                |
| `media`      | `@postkit/react/kits/media`      | Audio, Carousel, Device, Figure, Gallery, Video                                                                  |
| `discovery`  | `@postkit/react/kits/discovery`  | AppearsOn, AuthorCard, LinkPreview, RelatedContent, SeriesNavigation, SocialPost                                 |
| `engagement` | `@postkit/react/kits/engagement` | CallToAction, NewsletterSignup, Poll, ShareActions                                                               |
| `publishing` | `@postkit/react/kits/publishing` | ProductCard, SponsorBlock                                                                                        |

All six are also exported together from `@postkit/react/kits`, and as one
array, `postkitKits`. Each component page shows which kit it belongs to.
[Footnote](/components/footnote) and [Footnotes](/components/footnotes) are
in `article`, and [Footnotes](/docs/footnotes) covers how to write them.

## Turn kits on

Pass the kits to `createPostkit`:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, technical } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, technical],
});
```

Kits are renderer-neutral. They list definitions, and each renderer package
supplies the views for them, so the same kits work with the Chakra renderer:

```ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, technical, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';
import { chakra } from '@postkit/chakra';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article, technical, media],
});
```

## Leave one out

Use `exclude` to drop a component from a kit you otherwise want:

```ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, engagement } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, engagement],
  exclude: ['Poll'],
});
```

## What a kit changes

The set you enable is the set everything else uses:

- `postkit.mdxComponents` contains only the enabled components, plus prose.
- `postkit.remarkPlugins` validates directives against the enabled set, so a
  post that uses a component you didn't turn on fails the build the same way a
  misspelled one does (see [Validation](/docs/validation)).
- `postkit.manifest()` describes exactly the enabled set, so editors like
  Prismark offer writers only what your site renders.

An excluded or not-enabled component fails strict validation like an
unknown one, and the error says it isn't enabled. With `strict: false` it's a
warning, as for any unknown component.

Every built-in component has a view in both renderers, so every kit works
with either one. If a renderer has no view for an enabled component, as can
happen with a third-party renderer, the component stays out of the manifest,
and using it fails the build in every mode with an error naming it. Give it a
view with `overrides`, or add it to `exclude`.

## Add your own

Your own components and third-party packages join the set through
`components`, next to the kits. See [New components](/docs/new-components).

## Compatibility

You can still import components one at a time: the `@postkit/react` root
exports every headless view, and the `@postkit/chakra` root every Chakra view.
Kits are the recommended way to choose a set, because they also set what is
validated and what the manifest describes.

## MDX

Source: /docs/mdx

Use JSX declarations in MDX:

```mdx
<Callout title="Release status" tone="tip">
  The content remains regular **Markdown**.
</Callout>

<Audio src="/media/episode.mp3" title="Episode 12" />
```

Register Postkit's component map with the framework's MDX runtime. Framework
adapters supply the same components with native internal-link behavior:

```tsx
import { createPostkitMdxComponents } from '@postkit/chakra';

export const mdxComponents = createPostkitMdxComponents();
```

MDX is executable JavaScript. Compile it only from authors trusted at that
level; for untrusted authoring, use [Markdown directives](/docs/markdown-directives)
instead (see [Security](/docs/security)).

## Code blocks

Fenced code blocks are automatically rendered with Postkit's Chakra CodeBlock
component. They have plain-text output, copying, wrapping, and line-number
support without requiring a syntax-highlighting dependency.

By default, non-empty blocks show `"Copy code"`, line numbers are hidden, and
long lines remain unwrapped with horizontal scrolling. Set site-wide behavior
without replacing the Markdown component map:

```tsx
<PostkitProvider
  codeBlock={{
    colorScheme: 'light',
    copy: true,
    lineNumbers: false,
    size: 'md',
    variant: 'outline',
    wrap: false,
  }}
>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>
```

Direct `CodeBlock` props override provider configuration, and provider
configuration overrides Postkit's neutral defaults. Chakra CodeBlock defaults
the highlighting color scheme to `"dark"` when it is not configured.

Hosts that want syntax highlighting can install `@postkit/shiki`, create its
lazy adapter once at module scope, and pass it to `PostkitProvider`:

```tsx
import { PostkitProvider } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { createPostkitShikiAdapter } from '@postkit/shiki';

const codeBlockAdapter = createPostkitShikiAdapter();

<PostkitProvider codeBlockAdapter={codeBlockAdapter}>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>;
```

`@postkit/shiki` provides practical language and light/dark theme defaults.
Pass `languages` and `themes` when an application wants a smaller or customized
bundle. Chakra loads the adapter once and reuses it for nested code blocks. The
adapter uses Shiki's JavaScript regex engine, so no WebAssembly is downloaded;
pass `engine: 'oniguruma'` for a grammar that needs it. A fence in a language
that isn't loaded renders as plain text instead of failing.

## Customize code-copy feedback

Fenced code blocks inherit copy-control content from `PostkitProvider`. This
keeps site icons and labels outside authored Markdown while retaining Chakra's
Button recipe and clipboard behavior:

```tsx
<PostkitProvider
  codeBlock={{
    copyAriaLabel: 'Copy code',
    copyFeedback: 'tooltip',
    copyIcon: <ClipboardIcon aria-hidden="true" />,
    copyLabel: null,
    copiedIcon: <CheckIcon aria-hidden="true" />,
    copiedLabel: 'Copied!',
  }}
>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>
```

With `copyFeedback: 'tooltip'`, the control swaps to `copiedIcon` and shows the
copied label in a tooltip without changing the button's width. Chakra's default
check icon is used when `copiedIcon` is omitted. Leave `copyFeedback` unset for
the default inline icon-and-label behavior.

Direct `CodeBlock` props with the same names override these provider defaults.
Use `null` to suppress a provider label or icon for one block. Both feedback
modes announce the copied label through a polite live region.

## Configure individual fences

When the Markdown compiler forwards fence metadata through `meta`,
`metastring`, or `data-meta`, Postkit recognizes safe literal options:

````md
```tsx title="button.tsx" lineNumbers wrap {2-3} maxHeight="24rem"
export function Button() {
  return <button>Save</button>;
}
```
````

Supported options are `title`/`filename`, `lineNumbers`/`noLineNumbers`,
`wrap`/`noWrap`, highlighted ranges such as `{1,3-5}`, and validated
`maxHeight` lengths. Pipeline adapters can instead emit `data-title`,
`data-filename`, `data-line-numbers`, `data-wrap`, `data-highlight-lines`, and
`data-max-height`. Explicit attributes take precedence over the metadata
string. CSS expressions and authored JavaScript are rejected.

## Choose one syntax per file

MDX interprets braces as JavaScript expressions. Use JSX in `.mdx` files and
reserve `::postkit-*{...}` declarations for plain Markdown pipelines (see
[Markdown directives](/docs/markdown-directives)).

## Markdown directives

Source: /docs/markdown-directives

Plain Markdown pipelines can use literal-only directives:

```md
:::postkit-callout{title="Release status" tone="tip"}
The content remains regular **Markdown**.
:::
```

Directive props are literal values rather than arbitrary JavaScript, which
keeps the format portable and suitable for untrusted authoring environments.

## Enable the Remark preset

Add Postkit's Remark plugins to the Markdown pipeline:

```ts
import { createPostkitRemarkPlugins } from '@postkit/chakra/remark';

export const markdownOptions = {
  remarkPlugins: createPostkitRemarkPlugins(),
};
```

The preset enables GitHub Flavored Markdown, frontmatter recognition, the
directive syntax, and the Postkit transform. Pass options to adjust it:

- `before` and `after` add Remark plugins around Postkit's defaults.
- `gfm: false` or `frontmatter: false` omits that default.
- `postkit: { output: 'hast' }` annotates directives for pipelines such as
  react-markdown that map `data.hName` to a registered component. The default
  output is MDX JSX nodes.
- `postkit: { footnotes: { defaults } }` sets your site's footnote settings,
  and `postkit: { footnotes: false }` leaves GFM's own footnotes alone (see
  [Footnotes](#footnotes)).

With [`createPostkit`](/docs/create-postkit), use `postkit.remarkPlugins`
instead: it's the same preset, validating against the components your kits
enable, and takes the same options through `createPostkit({ remark })`.

The focused `@postkit/chakra/remark` entry point keeps React components and
Chakra theme declarations out of build-only Markdown tooling. Existing root
imports remain supported.

## Directive forms

Every component has a `postkit-` directive name, listed on its
[component page](/components).

- Components with Markdown children use a container directive with three
  colons, closed by a matching `:::` line.
- Components without children use a leaf directive with two colons on a
  single line.

```md
::postkit-audio{src="/media/episode.mp3" title="Episode 12"}

::postkit-link-preview{href="https://example.com/article"}
```

Props that take a list, such as the `items` of `Tabs` or `Carousel`, take a
JSON array written as a literal string:

```md
::postkit-tabs{items='[{"label":"npm","content":"npm install @postkit/chakra"},{"label":"pnpm","content":"pnpm add @postkit/chakra"}]'}
```

## Footnotes

Footnotes use GitHub's syntax: a `[^id]` reference in the text, and a `[^id]:`
note anywhere in the file.

```md
Postkit numbers notes by first reference.[^order] A note can be referenced
again.[^order]

[^order]: The id is a name, never a number: the reader sees 1, 2, 3.
```

A short note can go inline with the `:footnote` text directive:

```md
Directives never run code.:footnote[They take literal strings and JSON.]
```

The notes close the document. To place the list somewhere else, or change its
settings for one document, put a `::footnotes` leaf directive where it goes:

```md
::footnotes{title="Sources" numbering="lower-roman"}
```

They become Postkit's `Footnote` and `Footnotes` components whenever those
are enabled; with `createPostkit`, they're in the `article` kit. A reference with no note fails the build, and a note nobody
references is a warning. See [Footnotes](/docs/footnotes) for placement,
settings and styling.

## Validation

Directives are validated against the component declarations while the
Markdown is transformed. By default the transform throws when a directive:

- uses a prop the component does not declare;
- gives an enum prop a value outside its allowed values;
- omits a required prop.

This makes malformed authored content fail a site build instead of silently
changing behavior. Errors name the line and column, and the file when the build
passes one.

A directive that uses the `postkit-` prefix but names no Postkit component also
fails the build in strict mode (the default), and warns when `strict` is off.
Anything else that only looks like a directive stays literal text, so ratios
like 4.5:1, times like 10:30 and URLs with ports render as written. See
[Validation](/docs/validation) for the full rules.

## Choose one syntax per file

MDX interprets braces as JavaScript expressions, which conflicts with the
brace-attribute syntax of directives. Use JSX in `.mdx` files (see
[MDX](/docs/mdx)) and reserve `::postkit-*{...}` declarations for plain
Markdown pipelines.

## Validation

Source: /docs/validation

Postkit checks authored components when a post compiles, so a misspelled prop,
an impossible value or a misspelled component stops the build instead of
reaching a reader. This page describes what is checked and what each error
means.

## What gets checked

Directives, and the component names used in MDX, are validated by Postkit's
Remark plugin. It is part of the preset from `createPostkitRemarkPlugins()`,
which also enables GFM, frontmatter and the directive syntax:

```ts
import { createPostkitRemarkPlugins } from '@postkit/chakra/remark';

export const remarkPlugins = createPostkitRemarkPlugins();
```

The same preset is exported from `@postkit/react/remark`. With
[`createPostkit`](/docs/create-postkit), use `postkit.remarkPlugins`, which
validates against exactly the components your [kits](/docs/kits) enable.

Each directive is matched to a component by its directive name, such as
`postkit-callout`, or by the component name in lowercase, such as `callout`.
Its attributes are then checked against that component's declared props:

| Check                      | Example                                | Error                                                            |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The prop exists            | `:::postkit-callout{mood="tip"}`       | `Unknown Callout prop "mood" in Postkit directive.`              |
| An enum value is allowed   | `:::postkit-callout{tone="tpi"}`       | `Invalid Callout tone value "tpi".`                              |
| JSON data is literal JSON  | `::postkit-tabs{items="[{label: 1}]"}` | `Invalid Tabs items value: expected literal JSON…`               |
| A number is a number       | `initialIndex="second"`                | `Invalid Tabs initialIndex value "second": …`                    |
| Required props are present | `::postkit-card-grid` with no `items`  | `Postkit CardGrid directive requires "items".`                   |
| The component is enabled   | `::postkit-poll` without its kit       | `Unknown Postkit directive "postkit-poll": Poll isn't enabled.…` |

Attribute values are literal strings. Directives never evaluate JavaScript, so
they're safe for untrusted authoring environments. A prop that takes data, such
as `items`, takes JSON: a JavaScript object literal fails the JSON check, and
in MDX a brace expression in directive attributes is rejected by the MDX parser
itself. Each component page lists its props, their allowed values and which
ones are required.

## Strict mode

Strict mode is on by default. It fails the build on anything Postkit doesn't
recognise: an unknown prop, an unknown `postkit-*` directive, an unknown MDX
component, or a built-in component your `createPostkit` set doesn't enable.
Turning it off reports those as warnings instead:

```ts
export const remarkPlugins = createPostkitRemarkPlugins({
  postkit: { strict: false },
});
```

With strict mode off, unknown props are dropped, and unknown directives and
components render as they did before. Invalid values, malformed JSON and
missing required props fail in both modes, and so does a
[footnote](#footnotes) reference with no note. Warnings are `VFileMessage`s on the
compiled file's `messages`; they don't stop the build, so check them if you
rely on them.

Keep strict mode on for anything you publish. A dropped prop or an ignored
component is a silent change to what the author asked for.

## Aliases and warnings

Some props accept another name. Callout's `tone` also answers to `type`, so
callouts written for other tools work as they are: `:::postkit-callout{type="tip"}`
is the same as `tone="tip"`. The alias is checked like the prop, and when both
are set the prop wins and the build reports a warning.

Some props are recommended rather than required. Leaving one out is a warning,
never an error, in every mode, strict included. Today that's `Video`'s
`captions`: a video without a captions track warns, in the build output and in
the browser console during development, unless you mark it `decorative` (a
silent loop, say) or pass `tracks`:

```text
Postkit Video: the "captions" prop is missing. Add a captions track (a WebVTT file), or mark the video decorative. (content/post.md:7:1-7:48)
```

These warnings carry the `ruleId` `recommended-prop`. In MDX, the check reads
the element's literal attributes, so `<Video src="/a.mp4" decorative />`
doesn't warn, and an element with a spread (`{...props}`) is left alone.

## Where an error points

Errors are reported through the file being compiled (`vfile.fail`), so MDX,
next-mdx-remote, content-collections and other unified hosts report them as
compile errors. Each message ends with the file and the
`line:column-line:column` range of the directive or component:

```text
Invalid Callout tone value "tpi". (content/post.md:3:1-5:4)
```

The error also carries `file`, `line`, `column`, `ruleId` (such as
`unknown-directive`, `invalid-prop`, `missing-prop`, `unknown-component` or
`missing-footnote`) and
`source: 'postkit'`. The file appears when your build passes a path to the
compiler, for example `compile({ path, value })`. When it passes the source as
a plain string, as next-mdx-remote's `serialize` does, the message carries the
line and column alone and your build tool names the page it was compiling.

## Unknown components

**In plain Markdown**, a directive with the `postkit-` prefix that doesn't
match a component, such as `:::postkit-calout`, fails a strict build:

```text
Unknown Postkit directive "postkit-calout". Check the name against the component catalog. (content/post.md:3:1-5:4)
```

A directive without the prefix that isn't a component is put back as the text
you wrote. That keeps a ratio like 4.5:1, a time like 10:30, `localhost:3000`
or `:smile_cat:` as text, instead of turning them into an empty block. If you
use other directive plugins, add them to the preset's `before` list: a
directive they've already handled (it carries `data.hName`) is left alone.

**In MDX**, a capitalised JSX element that isn't a Postkit component fails a
strict build:

```text
Unknown MDX component <Calout>: it isn't a Postkit component, imported by the document or listed in `components`. (content/post.mdx:3:1-3:33)
```

A built-in component your `createPostkit` set leaves out fails the same way,
and the error says so:

```text
Unknown MDX component <Poll>: Postkit's Poll isn't enabled. Add its kit to createPostkit, or remove it from `exclude`. (content/post.mdx:1:1-1:22)
```

Lowercase HTML elements, member expressions such as `<motion.div>`, and names
the document imports or exports are always accepted. If your site passes its
own components to MDX through the component map, list them:

```ts
export const remarkPlugins = createPostkitRemarkPlugins({
  postkit: { components: ['Showcase', 'SiteBanner'] },
});
```

## Props in MDX

The Remark plugin checks MDX component names, not their props (apart from the
recommended-prop warnings above). Props on JSX elements are passed to the
component as written, so an unknown prop or an out-of-range value on
`<Callout>` isn't caught at compile time.

The components check them when they render instead. In development, every
built-in view warns once in the browser console about a missing required prop
or a value of the wrong kind, and so does any view you build with
`postkitView` or `postkitChakraView`:

```text
Postkit Callout: the "tone" prop must be one of "note", "tip", "important", "warning", "caution"; received "tpi".
```

An enum value the component doesn't allow falls back to its default, so the
page still renders. Nothing is checked or logged in production. A few
components that take JSON data, such as `LinkPreview` and `SocialPost`, reject
malformed data when they render.

## Footnotes

Footnotes are checked when the post compiles (see [Footnotes](/docs/footnotes)):

| Check                              | Result  | Message                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A reference has a note             | Error   | `Footnote [^b] has no definition.`                                       |
| Every note is referenced           | Warning | `Footnote [^z] is defined but never referenced; it is left out.`         |
| A note is defined once             | Warning | `Footnote [^a] is defined more than once; the first definition is used.` |
| The list is placed once            | Warning | `Footnotes is placed more than once; the first placement is used.`       |
| `::footnotes` settings are allowed | Error   | `Invalid Footnotes placement value "middle".`                            |

The error fails the build in every mode, strict or not, and points at the
reference. The warnings carry the `ruleId` `unreferenced-footnote`,
`duplicate-footnote` or `duplicate-footnotes`.

## One syntax per file

MDX reads braces as JavaScript expressions. Use JSX in `.mdx` files and keep
`:::postkit-*` directives with their brace attributes for plain Markdown
pipelines. See [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) for other integration
problems.

## Footnotes

Source: /docs/footnotes

Footnotes are part of the portable document, so they survive every renderer:
your site, email, feeds and plain text. Authors write them once, and your site
decides where readers see them: at the end, in the margin, in a popover or
opened under the line.

They render as two components in the `article` [kit](/docs/kits):
[Footnote](/components/footnote), the mark in the text, and
[Footnotes](/components/footnotes), the list of notes.

## Write a footnote

Use GitHub's footnote syntax, in Markdown or MDX. A `[^id]` reference goes in
the text, and a `[^id]:` note can go anywhere in the file:

```md
Postkit numbers notes by first reference.[^order] A note can be referenced
more than once.[^order]

[^order]: The id is a name, not a number. Readers see 1, 2, 3.
```

A short note can go inline. In Markdown, use the `:footnote` text directive;
in MDX, the `Footnote` component with the note as its children:

```md
Directives never run code.:footnote[They take literal strings and JSON.]
```

```mdx
Directives never run code.<Footnote>They take literal strings and JSON.</Footnote>
```

Notes are numbered in the order they're first referenced. A note referenced
more than once is listed once, with a link back to each reference (↩, then
a, b, …). Ids are prefixed per document (`fn-{slug}-1`), so a feed or index
page that shows several posts never repeats one.

## Place the list

The list closes the document. To put it somewhere else, such as before an
author card, place it with a leaf directive in Markdown or the component in
MDX:

```md
::footnotes
```

```mdx
<Footnotes />
```

The placed list also takes settings for this one document:

```md
::footnotes{title="Sources" numbering="lower-roman"}
```

## Placement

`placement` decides where readers see the notes:

| Placement | What readers see                                                                              |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `end`     | The numbered list where the document places it, or at the end. The default.                   |
| `side`    | Sidenotes in the margin, each beside the line that references it.                             |
| `popover` | The note in a native `popover`, anchored to the mark, when the reader activates it.           |
| `inline`  | The note opened under its line when the reader activates the mark, with a button to close it. |

`popover` and `inline` enhance the end list and never replace it, so the notes
still print and are still there without JavaScript. `side` replaces the list on
screen and keeps it in print. It falls back to `end` below `sideBreakpoint`
(1024px by default), when the margin is too narrow for the notes, or when the
stacked notes would run past the end of the article.

Side notes sit in the inline-end margin, `--postkit-sidenote-width` (232px)
wide and `--postkit-sidenote-gap` (48px) from the text, so leave that much room
beside your article column. Each note starts at its reference's line, and a
note that would overlap the one before moves down below it. They share the
margin with [Aside](/components/aside).

### Responsive placement

Pass one placement per breakpoint, smallest first. postkit.org uses this for
its notes: opened in place on phones, end notes from `md`, and sidenotes from
`xl`:

```ts
{ base: 'inline', md: 'end', xl: 'side' }
```

The breakpoint names are `base`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl` and `2xl`. With
`@postkit/chakra` they're your Chakra system's breakpoints. The headless
`Footnotes` uses Chakra UI's defaults (480, 768, 1024, 1280 and 1536px), or
the widths you pass in its `breakpoints` prop. In a directive, write the
object as JSON:

```md
::footnotes{placement='{"base":"inline","md":"end","xl":"side"}'}
```

## Set your site's footnotes

Set the defaults for every document in the Remark options, so the settings
are written into each document's references and list:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { chakra } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article],
  remark: {
    postkit: {
      footnotes: {
        defaults: {
          placement: { base: 'inline', md: 'end', xl: 'side' },
          variant: 'plain',
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

Without `createPostkit`, pass the same `postkit` options to
`createPostkitRemarkPlugins`. `footnotes` also takes `scope`, the id prefix,
which defaults to the file's `data.slug` or front-matter `slug`, then its file
name. `footnotes: false` turns Postkit's handling off and leaves GFM's own
footnotes alone.

A document overrides the defaults with an authored `::footnotes{…}` or
`<Footnotes … />`, or with a `footnotes:` key in its front matter when your
pipeline puts the parsed front matter on `file.data.matter` or
`file.data.frontmatter`:

```yaml
footnotes:
  placement: side
```

You can also set `Footnotes` props in `createPostkit`'s
[`defaults`](/docs/defaults-and-slots). They apply when the page renders, and
each `Footnote` takes the shared settings (`marker`, `numbering`, `placement`,
`sideBreakpoint`) from them, so one setting styles both.

## Props

`Footnote` and `Footnotes` share these settings:

| Prop             | Values                                                    | Default       |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| `placement`      | `end`, `side`, `popover`, `inline`, or one per breakpoint | `end`         |
| `marker`         | `superscript`, `bracket` (`[1]` on the baseline), `pill`  | `superscript` |
| `numbering`      | `decimal`, `lower-roman`, `lower-alpha`, `symbol`         | `decimal`     |
| `sideBreakpoint` | A width in px, below which `side` falls back to `end`     | `1024`        |
| `size`           | `sm`, `md`, `lg`                                          | `md`          |
| `variant`        | `outline`, `subtle`, `plain`                              | `subtle`      |

`symbol` numbering uses \*, †, ‡, §, ‖ and ¶, then doubles them. In React,
`numbering` also takes a function from the note's number to its mark.

`Footnotes` also takes:

| Prop        | Values                                                                                 | Default   |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| `title`     | The list heading. `false` hides it, and the list keeps "Notes" as its accessible name. | `"Notes"` |
| `backlinks` | Whether each note links back to its references.                                        | `true`    |

The Markdown tooling sets the rest (`identifier`, `index`, `occurrence`,
`references` and `scope`), so authors never write them.

## Validation

A reference with no note fails the build, in every mode, and points at the
reference:

```text
Footnote [^b] has no definition. (content/post.md:3:6-3:10)
```

A note nobody references is left out with a warning, and so is a second note
with the same id, or a second `::footnotes`. An invalid `placement`, `marker`
or `numbering` on `::footnotes` fails like any invalid prop. See
[Validation](/docs/validation#footnotes).

## Style them

The parts are `root` and `marker` for `Footnote`, and `root`, `title`, `rule`,
`list`, `item`, `number`, `content` and `backlink` for `Footnotes`. Style them
like any other component (see [Part styles](/docs/part-styles)).

With the headless renderer and `@postkit/react/styles.css`, these custom
properties retheme them:

| Custom property                                                     | Sets                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `--postkit-footnote-accent`                                         | The highlighted sidenote's rule    |
| `--postkit-footnote-marker-color`, `--postkit-footnote-marker-size` | The mark in the text               |
| `--postkit-footnote-number-color`, `--postkit-footnote-number-size` | The number beside each note        |
| `--postkit-footnote-text-color`, `--postkit-footnote-text-size`     | The notes' text                    |
| `--postkit-footnote-rule`, `--postkit-footnote-rule-width`          | The rule above the list            |
| `--postkit-footnote-target-bg`                                      | The note a reader just jumped to   |
| `--postkit-sidenote-width`, `--postkit-sidenote-gap`                | The margin column (232px and 48px) |

With `@postkit/chakra`, the sizes and the sidenote column read the same
custom properties, and the colours come from your system's semantic tokens.
Restyle them with `createPostkitTheme({ footnote, footnotes, sidenote })`,
like any recipe (see [Tokens](/docs/tokens)).

Every mark is a link to its note with `role="doc-noteref"` and a label such as
"Note 1", with a tap target of at least 24px. Activating a mark moves focus
to its note, a backlink returns it to the mark, and Escape closes a note opened
in place.

## In other renderers

| Renderer                      | Footnotes                                                                                    |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Headless and Chakra           | Every placement, with the shared behaviour (`useFootnotes` in `@postkit/react`).             |
| [Email](/docs/email)          | Always end notes: superscript numbers without links, and a numbered "Notes" list at the end. |
| Static HTML (`@postkit/core`) | The end list, with links and backlinks.                                                      |
| Plain text (`@postkit/core`)  | `[1]` marks, and a `[1] Note` list where the list is placed, or at the end.                  |

Email leaves out the links because in-message anchors are unreliable across
mail clients.

## Portable documents and feeds

Source: /docs/portable-documents

Use `@postkit/core` when an API or feed needs to offer the same article as
HTML, Markdown, MDX, or versioned JSON. The package has no React dependency.

```ts
import { parsePostkit, serializePostkit } from '@postkit/core';

const document = parsePostkit(input, { format: 'html' });

return {
  html: serializePostkit(document, { format: 'html' }),
  markdown: serializePostkit(document, { format: 'markdown' }),
  json: serializePostkit(document, { format: 'json' }),
};
```

The HTML parser keeps safe semantic structure and strips scripts, event
handlers, presentation attributes, and executable URLs. The safe MDX parser
accepts literal component tags but rejects expressions, spread props, imports,
and exports. JSON input must match the current versioned document schema.

Task lists retain checked and unchecked state through HTML using disabled
checkboxes. Markdown exports escape literal block markers, entities, and link
destinations to preserve their meaning. Footnotes are portable: `[^id]` and
`:footnote[…]` become `footnoteReference` and `footnoteDefinition` nodes,
numbered by first reference. HTML gets linked marks and an end list with
backlinks (ids prefixed by `footnotes.scope`), plain text gets `[1]` marks
and a numbered list, and a reference with no definition fails with its line
and column.

## Render through Chakra

`@postkit/chakra/document` supplies `DocumentRenderer`. Semantic input is mapped
through Postkit's Chakra-backed prose primitives, so the host's Heading, List,
Table, Image, Code, and other recipes continue to apply.

```tsx
import { DocumentRenderer, parsePostkitHtml } from '@postkit/chakra/document';

const document = parsePostkitHtml(rssItem.content);

<PostkitProvider system={siteSystem}>
  <DocumentRenderer
    document={document}
    components={{
      a: SiteLink,
      img: FeedImage,
    }}
  />
</PostkitProvider>;
```

The renderer never creates arbitrary elements or invokes unknown components.
Unknown nodes are unwrapped by default, retaining readable children. Use the
`unknownElements` and `unknownComponents` props to drop them instead.

## Reconstruct rendered output

HTML serialization and `DocumentRenderer` emit versioned `data-postkit-*`
annotations by default. They identify semantic nodes, rich component names,
and JSON-compatible component props without requiring an extra layout wrapper.
`parsePostkitHtml` recognizes those hints, while also remaining useful for
ordinary unannotated RSS or CMS HTML.

Annotations improve round trips, but they are not an authenticity mechanism.
Continue to treat remote content as untrusted and expose only application-
approved component overrides and link behavior.

## Link previews and unfurling

Source: /docs/link-previews

Remote content is normalized before rendering. `@postkit/unfurl` returns a
provider-neutral snapshot; `LinkPreview` and `SocialPost` render that snapshot.
This keeps remote requests, credentials, and provider-specific response formats
out of presentation components.

`@postkit/unfurl` normalizes metadata from Open Graph, oEmbed, OpenGraphs, and
custom resolvers. It is designed for a server or build process, not direct use
in a browser component.

## Resolution flow

1. The application receives or loads a URL.
2. A trusted server validates it against the application's URL policy.
3. `@postkit/unfurl` calls the configured provider.
4. The application caches the normalized result.
5. A Postkit component renders the normalized snapshot.

Provider credentials remain at the resolver boundary.

## Create a resolver

Adapters are included for OpenGraphs, Iframely, Embedly, and Microlink. Every
adapter normalizes its response into `ResolvedLinkPreview`. OpenGraphs is the
default provider when a registry is created:

```ts
import {
  createIframelyResolver,
  createLinkResolverRegistry,
  createOpenGraphsResolver,
} from '@postkit/unfurl';

export const linkResolver = createLinkResolverRegistry({
  resolvers: [
    createOpenGraphsResolver({
      apiKey: process.env.OPENGRAPHS_API_KEY,
    }),
    createIframelyResolver({
      apiKey: process.env.IFRAMELY_API_KEY!,
    }),
  ],
  fallbackProviders: ['iframely'],
});

const metadata = await linkResolver.resolve('https://example.com/article');
```

Fallback providers are opt-in, so an outage or malformed response does not
unexpectedly consume credits with another service. Use
`createCallbackResolver` to wrap an application's own resolution function.

## Rendering

`LinkPreview` can consume a normalized link result through its `metadata`
prop, either as an object or as a JSON string from a saved snapshot:

```tsx
<LinkPreview href="https://example.com/article" metadata={metadata} />
```

The card's title is a paragraph, because a preview can't know where it sits
in your page's outline. When it should be a heading, say which one with
`headingLevel` (`2` to `6`), so it follows the heading above it. `Chart` and
`Carousel` take the same prop for their titles.

```tsx
<LinkPreview href="https://example.com/article" headingLevel={3} />
```

`SocialPost` can render a captured social snapshot or use an application
callback to resolve one at runtime.

Live embeds should remain an explicit application choice because they can add
third-party scripts, tracking, consent requirements, and layout instability.
Provider markup is retained as `embed.rawHtml`, but Postkit's React renderer
never injects it. See [Security](/docs/security) for the full trust boundary.

## Tokens

Source: /docs/tokens

Postkit is host-native by default. Its semantic components use Chakra
primitives internally, so an existing application's tokens and recipes flow
through. Postkit adds no visual preset unless the host opts into one. The
`Prose` wrapper still provides structural content rhythm in either mode.

## Layer a system

```tsx
import { createSystem, defaultConfig } from '@chakra-ui/react';
import { PostkitProvider } from '@postkit/chakra';
import {
  createPostkitSystem,
  createPostkitTheme,
  postkitDefaultTheme,
} from '@postkit/chakra/theme';

const siteSystem = createSystem(defaultConfig, {
  theme: {
    tokens: {
      fonts: {
        body: { value: '"Inter", sans-serif' },
        heading: { value: '"Newsreader", serif' },
        mono: { value: '"JetBrains Mono", monospace' },
      },
    },
  },
});

const system = createPostkitSystem({
  system: siteSystem,
  // Optional. Omit this when the host supplies all visual policy.
  preset: postkitDefaultTheme,
  theme: createPostkitTheme({
    prose: { base: { p: { fontSize: 'lg' } } },
  }),
});

<PostkitProvider system={system}>{article}</PostkitProvider>;
```

The layering order is:

1. The optional `preset`, such as `postkitDefaultTheme`
2. The site-wide Chakra `system`
3. The explicit `theme` supplied to the nearest `PostkitProvider`

`PostkitProvider` accepts the same three props directly, so a site can pass
`system`, `preset`, and `theme` there instead of composing a system first.

Import theme-only APIs from `@postkit/chakra/theme`. This focused entry point
keeps component and Markdown declarations out of shared theme libraries and
reduces cold TypeScript work. Existing imports from `@postkit/chakra` remain
supported.

## Choose a styling mode

- Host-native: pass the site's `system` and omit `preset`. Chakra primitive
  recipes and any host-registered Postkit slot recipes control presentation;
  wrapper-owned prose spacing and semantic technical-content structure remain
  active.
- Standalone preset: pass `preset={postkitDefaultTheme}` for Postkit's complete
  visual treatment, including its dark CodeBlock, CodeGroup, and Terminal
  palettes.
- Scoped customization: add `theme={createPostkitTheme(...)}` to either mode.

## Typography

Postkit components use three font roles: `body` for prose, descriptions, and
controls; `heading` for titles and heading-like slots; and `mono` for code. In
a host system they come from the `fonts` tokens. To change them only inside a
Postkit subtree, pass `typography` to `createPostkitTheme`:

```tsx
const theme = createPostkitTheme({
  typography: {
    body: '"Inter", sans-serif',
    heading: ['"Newsreader"', 'serif'],
    mono: '"JetBrains Mono", monospace',
  },
});
```

## Tune prose rhythm

External spacing belongs to the `Prose` wrapper rather than the individual
Heading, paragraph, table, or code components. Eight custom properties provide
the default flow and internal list scales and can be changed through a scoped
Postkit theme:

```tsx
const documentationTheme = createPostkitTheme({
  prose: {
    base: {
      root: {
        '--postkit-prose-flow-space': 'spacing.5',
        '--postkit-prose-block-space': 'spacing.8',
        '--postkit-prose-section-space': 'spacing.10',
        '--postkit-prose-heading-space': 'spacing.12',
        '--postkit-prose-title-space': 'spacing.16',
        '--postkit-prose-list-indent': 'spacing.8',
        '--postkit-prose-list-item-space': 'spacing.2',
        '--postkit-prose-list-item-indent': 'spacing.1',
      },
    },
  },
});

<PostkitProvider system={siteSystem} theme={documentationTheme}>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>;
```

The wrapper applies these defaults before its prose recipe and direct `css`
prop, preserving both theme-level and instance-level overrides. Use
`<Prose unstyled>` for a completely bare wrapper.

To restyle individual parts of a component, see [Part styles](/docs/part-styles).

## Part styles

Source: /docs/part-styles

Every Postkit component is built from named parts (slots). A `Callout` has
`root`, `icon`, `content`, `title`, and `body`; a `CodeBlock` has a title,
language label, copy control, and code lines. Each part can be styled at three
levels: the host's Chakra recipes, a scoped Postkit theme, or a single
instance.

## Host recipes flow through

Postkit's semantic components compose Chakra primitives, so the host's
Heading, Link, Button, Input, Table, Tabs, Code, and related recipes apply
without extra configuration.

Markdown headings render through Chakra `Heading` with `as="h1"` through
`as="h6"`. Postkit does not override the Heading recipe's font weight, family,
line height, letter spacing, or color. Markdown blockquotes and semantic lists,
including lists inside publishing components, render through Chakra
`Blockquote` and `List`. Code-block copy actions similarly render through
Chakra `Button` while retaining Postkit's copy behavior.

Structured controls also retain their Chakra recipe boundaries:
`NewsletterSignup` composes `Field`, `PullQuote` composes `Blockquote`, `Stat`
composes `Stat`, poll result bars compose `Progress`, and product ratings
compose a read-only `RatingGroup`.

Card-like surfaces use Chakra `Card` roots and parts where their content model
matches, author imagery uses `Avatar`, callouts and takeaways use `Alert`, and
responsive video or embed frames use `AspectRatio`. Postkit retains semantic
`article` and `aside` roots through Chakra's polymorphic rendering. Carousels
delegate paging, pointer dragging, and accessible controls to Chakra
`Carousel`, so the host's Carousel recipe flows through while Postkit retains
its article item model and content slots. Instructional `Steps` compose Chakra
`List`, allowing the host List recipe to flow through beneath Postkit's numbered
marker treatment. `Disclosure` intentionally remains native `details` and
`summary`, preserving built-in toggle behavior without client-side JavaScript.

## Scoped slot recipes

`createPostkitTheme` builds component-scoped slot recipe overrides for the
`theme` prop on `PostkitProvider`. Each component key accepts `base`,
`variants`, `defaultVariants`, and `compoundVariants`, keyed by slot name:

```tsx
import { PostkitProvider } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { createPostkitTheme } from '@postkit/chakra/theme';

const theme = createPostkitTheme({
  callout: {
    base: {
      title: { fontWeight: 'semibold', letterSpacing: '-0.01em' },
    },
    variants: {
      tone: {
        tip: { root: { borderInlineStartWidth: '4px' } },
      },
    },
  },
});

<PostkitProvider system={siteSystem} theme={theme}>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>;
```

The override applies only beneath that provider, so a documentation or
editorial subtree can differ from the rest of the site without changing
site-wide component defaults. To register Postkit slot recipes in the host
system itself, use the recipe names in `postkitRecipeKeys` (for example
`postkitRecipeKeys.callout` is `postkitCallout`).

## One instance

Components accept `slotStyles` for per-instance part styles, `rootProps` for
the root element, and `unstyled` to drop the component's recipe entirely:

```tsx
<Callout
  title="Heads up"
  tone="warning"
  slotStyles={{ title: { textTransform: 'uppercase' } }}
/>
```

Use content props for semantic variation and theme recipes for persistent
visual policy. Repeating `slotStyles` across articles is a sign the style
belongs in a theme.

## CodeBlock parts

CodeBlock's canonical content-specific slots are `title`, `language`,
`control`, `copyTrigger`, `copyIndicator`, `content`, `code`, `codeText`,
`line`, and `lineNumber`. The older `filename`, `actions`, `button`, `scroller`,
and `lineContent` slot names remain compatibility aliases.

## Lists

Markdown `ul`, `ol`, and `li` elements render through Chakra's List recipe;
pass `unstyled` to a mapped list root when its complete list subtree should be
bare. Ordered-list mappings retain native `start`, `reversed`, and `type`
attributes supplied by Markdown renderers.

## Defaults and slots

Source: /docs/defaults-and-slots

Defaults and slots are rungs 4 and 5 of the customization ladder. Both keep the
component's definition, so its directive, validation and manifest entry don't
change and every existing post keeps working.

| Rung            | What you change                    | How                                                    |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1. Props        | One instance                       | `variant`, `size`, `tone`, `layout`…                   |
| 2. Tokens       | Fonts, colours, spacing everywhere | Your Chakra system, or `--postkit-*` custom properties |
| 3. Part styles  | A component's look                 | Recipes, CSS on the anatomy, or `classNames` per part  |
| **4. Defaults** | What authors get without asking    | `defaults` in `createPostkit`                          |
| **5. Slots**    | One part of the markup             | `overrides.Callout.slots`                              |
| 6. Views        | The whole render                   | `overrides.Figure.view`                                |
| 7. Eject        | The source itself                  | `npx postkit eject`                                    |
| 8. New          | Something Postkit doesn't have     | `npx postkit new`                                      |

## Defaults

Set site-wide prop defaults with `defaults`, keyed by component name:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article],
  defaults: {
    Callout: { variant: 'plain' },
  },
});
```

Every callout now renders with the plain variant unless its author asks for
another one. A prop written in the post always wins over a default.

Without `defaults`, every component uses its definition's defaults. The
`variant` default is `subtle` for every component.

`createPostkit` checks `defaults` when it runs: a component that isn't
enabled, a prop the component doesn't have, or a value the prop doesn't allow
throws an error naming it.

The [manifest](/docs/manifest)'s per-prop `default` is the definition's
default, not your site's: the manifest describes the components, and your
defaults are a rendering choice.

### How each renderer applies them

The same `defaults` object works with both renderers:

- **Headless:** the defaults become the view's prop defaults.
- **Chakra:** props that are theme variants (`variant`, `size`, `tone`) are
  written into the recipe's `defaultVariants`. Other props become the view's
  defaults.

If you set the same variant default in both places, `createPostkit`'s
`defaults` wins.

Because Chakra variant defaults live in the recipe, you can also set them with
[part styles](/docs/part-styles), next to the rest of a component's look:

```ts
import { createPostkitTheme } from '@postkit/chakra';

export const postkitTheme = createPostkitTheme({
  callout: {
    defaultVariants: { variant: 'plain' },
  },
});
```

Use `defaults` when the choice is about content, and the recipe when it's part
of a theme you share between sites.

## Slots

A slot override replaces one named part of a component and keeps the rest.
The part names are the component's anatomy, listed on each component page.

```tsx
// lib/postkit.tsx
import { createPostkit, type PostkitSlotProps } from '@postkit/react';
import { article } from '@postkit/react/kits';

function InkMark(props: PostkitSlotProps) {
  return (
    <span {...props}>
      <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16" height="16">
        <circle cx="8" cy="8" r="6" fill="currentColor" />
      </svg>
    </span>
  );
}

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article],
  overrides: {
    Callout: {
      slots: { icon: InkMark },
    },
  },
});
```

Your part receives the slot's props and styles, typed as `PostkitSlotProps`:
the anatomy attributes (`data-postkit-part` and any state), the part's
`className` and `style`, and its children. With Chakra, the recipe's styles
for that part arrive in `className` too. Spread them onto your root element
so the part still carries its name and still picks up your CSS.

Class names per part, without replacing the element, go in
`overrides.Callout.classNames` (see [Part styles](/docs/part-styles)).

Slots replace the parts a view renders itself: an element the view returns
with a matching `data-postkit-part`. A view not built with
`postkitView` or `postkitChakraView` (in 0.3.0, Chakra's `CodeBlock`,
`CodeGroup`, `LinkPreview` and `SocialPost`) can't take slot overrides yet,
and `createPostkit` says so; override its view instead.

## When to go further

If you need to change how the parts fit together, not just one of them,
replace the whole render with a [view](/docs/views). If you need to change the
source itself, [eject](/docs/eject) it.

## Views

Source: /docs/views

A view is the render function for a component. Replacing it is rung 6 of the
customization ladder: you change the whole markup, and the component keeps its
definition. Its props, directive, validation and manifest entry stay the same,
so posts and Prismark don't notice the swap.

Reach for a view when [defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots) aren't
enough, for example when the parts need a different structure, not just a
different look.

## Build a view

Build the view with `postkitView` and the component's definition. The
definition gives your render function typed props and a `part` helper:

```tsx
// lib/postkit/figure.tsx
import { figureDefinition } from '@postkit/core/components';
import { postkitView } from '@postkit/react';

export const CommuneFigure = postkitView(
  figureDefinition,
  ({ props, part }) => (
    <figure {...part('root')}>
      <img {...part('image')} src={props.src} alt={props.alt} />
      {props.caption && (
        <figcaption {...part('figcaption')}>
          <span {...part('caption')}>{props.caption}</span>
        </figcaption>
      )}
    </figure>
  ),
);
```

`part(name)` returns everything a part needs: its anatomy attributes
(`data-postkit-component` and the theme-variant state on the root,
`data-postkit-part` on every part), its `classNames` entry, its `slotStyles`
and, on the root, `rootProps`. With Chakra it also returns the recipe's class
and styles. The part names are typed from the definition, so a misspelled part
doesn't compile.

`postkitView` also does the work every view needs. It applies `unstyled`,
fills in your site's defaults and then the definition's, so a prop with a
default is never `undefined`, maps aliases such as Callout's `type` to their
prop, and swaps in any [slot overrides](/docs/defaults-and-slots). In
development it warns once in the console about a missing required prop or a
value of the wrong kind.

## Use it

Register the view as an override:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';

import { CommuneFigure } from './postkit/figure';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, media],
  overrides: {
    Figure: { view: CommuneFigure },
  },
});
```

## Chakra views

With the Chakra renderer, build the view with `postkitChakraView`, which also
takes the component's recipe. Parts then get the recipe's slot styles and your
system's tokens:

```tsx
// lib/postkit/callout.tsx
import { Alert, Box } from '@chakra-ui/react';
import { postkitCalloutRecipe, postkitChakraView } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { calloutDefinition } from '@postkit/core/components';
import { postkitCalloutMarks } from '@postkit/react';

const toneStatus = {
  note: 'info',
  tip: 'success',
  important: 'neutral',
  warning: 'warning',
  caution: 'error',
} as const;

export const InkCallout = postkitChakraView(
  calloutDefinition,
  postkitCalloutRecipe,
  ({ props, part }) => (
    <Alert.Root as="aside" status={toneStatus[props.tone]} {...part('root')}>
      <Alert.Indicator aria-hidden="true" {...part('icon')}>
        {postkitCalloutMarks[props.tone]}
      </Alert.Indicator>
      <Alert.Content {...part('content')}>
        {props.title && (
          <Alert.Title {...part('title')}>{props.title}</Alert.Title>
        )}
        <Box {...part('body')}>{props.children}</Box>
      </Alert.Content>
    </Alert.Root>
  ),
);
```

Postkit's own Chakra Callout is written the same way. `@postkit/chakra`
exports each built-in recipe as `postkit<Name>Recipe`, such as
`postkitCalloutRecipe`, with its part names as `postkit<Name>Slots`.

The view uses the recipe your Chakra system registers under the recipe key
(`postkitCallout`) when there is one, so `createPostkitTheme` overrides still
apply. Without one, the parts keep the recipe's class names and render
unstyled; pass `{ fallback: 'recipe' }` as a fourth argument to apply the
recipe you passed instead, or `{ recipeKey }` to read another key.

## Keep the anatomy

Emit each part you render with `part(name)`, under the definition's name for
it. The part names are what [part styles](/docs/part-styles), slot overrides
and other renderers rely on, so a part your view drops or renders without
`part()` loses the styles and overrides aimed at it. The Figure view above,
for example, leaves out the credit, link and figure-number parts, so styles
for those have nothing to apply to.

## Views or eject

A view starts from nothing. If you want to start from Postkit's own view and
change it, [eject](/docs/eject) it instead: you get the source in your repo,
already wired up as an override.

## Eject

Source: /docs/eject

Ejecting is rung 7 of the customization ladder. It copies a component's view
(and its recipe, for Chakra) into your repo, so you own the source and can
change anything in it.

Unlike copying a component by hand, the contract stays upstream. An ejected
`Figure` still imports `figureDefinition` from `@postkit/core`, so its
directive, validation and manifest entry don't fork, and your posts, Prismark
and the email renderer keep treating it as a Figure.

## Eject a component

```sh
npx postkit eject figure --renderer chakra --to libs/postkit
```

```text
✓ libs/postkit/figure/figure.recipe.ts
✓ libs/postkit/figure/figure.tsx
✓ .postkit-eject.json   Figure @ @postkit/chakra 0.3.0
✓ lib/postkit.ts   overrides.Figure.view → ../libs/postkit/figure/figure

Still bound to Figure's definition from @postkit/core/components.
It imports @postkit/chakra, @postkit/core, @postkit/react; keep them in your dependencies.
Chakra applies the recipe registered as postkitFigure first: register the ejected recipe in your theme to use your edits (see /docs/eject).
Run `postkit diff figure` after upgrading @postkit/chakra.
```

The CLI copies that renderer's view from your installed `@postkit/chakra` or
`@postkit/react`, plus the recipe for Chakra and the CSS for headless, and
registers the copy as the component's [view](/docs/views) override in your
Postkit config:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { Figure } from '../libs/postkit/figure/figure';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article, media],
  overrides: { Figure: { view: Figure } },
});
```

It writes the import path the way your config already writes relative
imports, with `.js` if it uses `.js`. If it can't find your config, or can't
edit it safely, it prints those lines for you to add. See [CLI](/docs/cli#your-config) for how it finds the config
and for every flag.

| Flag            | Default       | Meaning                               |
| --------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `--renderer`    | from config   | `headless` or `chakra`                |
| `--to`          | `src/postkit` | Where the component's folder goes     |
| `--dry-run`     | `false`       | Show the files and config change only |
| `--force`       | `false`       | Overwrite files that already exist    |
| `--no-register` | registers     | Leave your config alone               |

### What the copy imports

The copied view imports its definition from `@postkit/core/components` and
helpers from the renderer package's public API (`@postkit/chakra`,
`@postkit/react`), so keep those in your dependencies. If a view needs a small
internal helper the package doesn't export, the helper is copied into an
`internal/` folder beside it.

### Using an ejected Chakra recipe

The ejected view passes its recipe to `postkitChakraView`, but Chakra uses the
recipe your system registers as `postkitFigure` first, and
`postkitDefaultTheme` registers Postkit's. To style the component with your
copy, register it last:

```tsx
import { defineConfig } from '@chakra-ui/react';
import { postkitDefaultTheme } from '@postkit/chakra';

import { postkitFigureRecipe } from '../libs/postkit/figure/figure.recipe';

const theme = defineConfig({
  theme: { slotRecipes: { postkitFigure: postkitFigureRecipe } },
});

<postkit.Provider preset={postkitDefaultTheme} theme={theme}>
  {children}
</postkit.Provider>;
```

## What stays upstream

| Ejected into your repo | Stays in Postkit                                      |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| The view               | The definition: props, directive, anatomy, validation |
| The recipe (Chakra)    | Behaviour, such as carousel paging or code copy       |
| The CSS (headless)     | The manifest entry                                    |

Behaviour lives in `@postkit/core/behaviors` and the renderer's hooks, so an
ejected interactive component keeps getting behaviour fixes when you upgrade.
And because the directive is validated against the upstream definition, a
post that passes a bad prop to `::postkit-figure` still fails the build with
your view in place.

## Keep up with upstream

`postkit eject` records what it copied in `.postkit-eject.json` at your
project root: the package, the version, a content hash and the upstream source
of each file. Commit it.

After an upgrade, `postkit diff` compares that recorded source with the
installed version's and prints a unified diff of what changed upstream, so
you can decide what to bring across. It never changes your copy, and it lists
the files you've edited since ejecting.

```sh
npx postkit diff figure
```

```text
Figure (chakra) in libs/postkit/figure: @postkit/chakra 0.3.0 → 0.3.2
--- a/figure.tsx	@postkit/chakra@0.3.0
+++ b/figure.tsx	@postkit/chakra@0.3.2
@@ -59,7 +59,7 @@
           alt={alt}
           htmlWidth={postkitImageDimension(props.width)}
           htmlHeight={postkitImageDimension(props.height)}
-          loading={props.loading}
+          loading={props.priority ? 'eager' : props.loading}
           decoding="async"
           sizes={props.sizes}
           srcSet={props.srcSet}

1 file changed upstream. Your copy wasn't changed.
Your edits: figure.recipe.ts.
```

When you've brought across what you want, `postkit diff figure --accept`
records the installed version as your new base, and your copy as it is now,
so later edits show against it. In CI, `postkit diff --exit-code` exits with
1 when an ejected component has upstream changes you haven't accepted.

## Before you eject

Ejecting is the last step before writing your own component. Most changes fit
lower on the ladder, where upgrades land without a diff:

- A different look: [Part styles](/docs/part-styles).
- Different defaults, or one part swapped: [Defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots).
- A new structure written from scratch: [Views](/docs/views).

See [CLI](/docs/cli) for every command.

## New components

Source: /docs/new-components

When Postkit doesn't have what you need, define it yourself. This is rung 8 of
the customization ladder. Your component is defined the same way Postkit's
built-in ones are, so it gets a Markdown directive, validation, theming and a
manifest entry for free, and Prismark can offer it to writers.

## Scaffold it

```sh
npx postkit new showcase --category media
```

```text
✓ src/postkit/showcase/showcase.definition.ts
✓ src/postkit/showcase/showcase.tsx
✓ src/postkit/showcase/showcase.css

Register it with createPostkit({ components }) in lib/postkit.ts:

import { Showcase } from '../src/postkit/showcase/showcase';
import { showcaseDefinition } from '../src/postkit/showcase/showcase.definition';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  // …your renderer and kits
  components: [{ definition: showcaseDefinition, view: Showcase }],
});

Use it as <Showcase /> in MDX or :::postkit-showcase in Markdown.
Import showcase.css from your global stylesheet for the headless view.
```

You get a definition, a headless view and its styles, as a starting point
that wraps authored content (`children: 'mdx'`), with a `title` prop and
`root`, `title` and `body` parts. `--chakra` adds a
Chakra view (`showcase.chakra.tsx`) and slot recipe (`showcase.recipe.ts`), and
`--spec` adds a spec per view. The CSS targets the anatomy attributes; import
it from your global stylesheet. See [CLI](/docs/cli#postkit-new) for every
flag.

In an Nx workspace, the generator writes the same files from the same
templates:

```sh
nx g @postkit/nx:component showcase --category=media --directory=libs/site/src/postkit
```

## Define it

The definition is the contract: the component's name, directive, props and
named parts. It's framework-free, so the manifest and editors can read it
without React. See [definePostkitComponent](/docs/define-postkit-component) for
every field.

The example frames a screenshot in a browser or app window. (Postkit's own
[Device](/components/device) already does iPhone, iPad and Mac frames.)

```ts
// showcase/showcase.definition.ts
import {
  definePostkitComponent,
  prop,
  presentation,
} from '@postkit/core/components';

export const showcaseDefinition = definePostkitComponent({
  name: 'Showcase',
  directive: 'postkit-showcase',
  category: 'media',
  description: 'A screenshot framed in a browser or app window.',
  runtime: 'static',
  stability: 'experimental',
  props: {
    ...presentation,
    kind: prop.enum(['browser', 'window'], {
      description: 'The showcase frame.',
      default: 'browser',
      themeVariant: true,
    }),
    src: prop.string('The screenshot URL.', { required: true }),
    alt: prop.string('Text alternative for the screenshot.', {
      required: true,
    }),
    caption: prop.string('An optional caption.'),
  },
  slots: ['root', 'frame', 'screen', 'caption'],
  keywords: ['showcase', 'screenshot', 'mockup'],
  example: {
    props: { kind: 'browser', src: '/shots/home.png', alt: 'The home page' },
  },
});
```

- **Required props** take `{ required: true }`. A directive without them
  fails validation, an MDX element without them gets a console warning in
  development, and the view receives them as non-optional.
- **`children`** can be left out, as here: it defaults to `'none'`. Set
  `children: 'mdx'` when the component wraps authored content.
- **`category`** is one of Postkit's six: `article-structure`,
  `technical-content`, `media`, `discovery`, `engagement` or `publishing`.
  Pick the closest; it groups the component in the manifest and in editors.

## Write the view

Build the view with `postkitView`, so it emits the anatomy and picks up
defaults, slot overrides and part styles like any other component:

```tsx
// showcase/showcase.tsx
import { postkitView } from '@postkit/react';

import { showcaseDefinition } from './showcase.definition';

export const Showcase = postkitView(showcaseDefinition, ({ props, part }) => (
  <figure {...part('root')}>
    <div {...part('frame')}>
      <img {...part('screen')} src={props.src} alt={props.alt} />
    </div>
    {props.caption && (
      <figcaption {...part('caption')}>{props.caption}</figcaption>
    )}
  </figure>
));
```

## Register it

Add the definition and view to `components`, next to your kits:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';

import { Showcase } from './showcase/showcase';
import { showcaseDefinition } from './showcase/showcase.definition';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, media],
  components: [{ definition: showcaseDefinition, view: Showcase }],
});
```

Writers can now use it in either syntax:

```mdx
<Showcase
  kind="window"
  src="/shots/editor.png"
  alt="The editor with a post open"
/>
```

```md
::postkit-showcase{kind="window" src="/shots/editor.png" alt="The editor with a post open"}
```

## What you get

From the one definition:

- Typed props for your view, with `PostkitPropsOf<typeof showcaseDefinition>`.
- A directive, validated like Postkit's own (see [Validation](/docs/validation)).
- An entry in `postkit.manifest()`, so editors like Prismark can offer it.
- Slot and variant types derived from its parts and theme-variant props, and
  the recipe key `postkitShowcase` if you write a Chakra view and recipe for it
  with `postkitChakraView`.
- Anatomy attributes on every part, so [part styles](/docs/part-styles) work
  the same as for built-in components.

## Share it

A component package exports `{ definition, view }` pairs and a manifest,
written with `createPostkitComponentManifest` from `@postkit/core/components`
(see [Manifest](/docs/manifest)). A site turns the components on by adding
those pairs to `components`, and editors read the manifest. A component that
proves itself can be proposed upstream to Postkit.

## Headless

Source: /docs/headless

`@postkit/react` is the headless renderer. Its views emit semantic markup,
landmarks and ARIA with a name on every part, and nothing else. You bring the
look with plain CSS, utility classes or any CSS-in-JS. There's no Chakra and no
Emotion in the bundle.

:::postkit-callout{tone="important" title="Upgrading from 0.2"}
From 0.3.0, `@postkit/react` is headless. The Chakra components that
`@postkit/react` exported in 0.2 are now in `@postkit/chakra`. To keep today's
look, install `@postkit/chakra` and change your imports. There's no
compatibility shim.
:::

## Install

