```sh
npm install @postkit/react react react-dom
```

It brings the definitions, the behaviour hooks, `createPostkit`, the kits, the
MDX map and the directive plugin with it.

The interactive components and hooks run on [Zag](https://zagjs.com). Zag is
an optional peer dependency, so a Chakra site uses the copy Chakra already
installs and never bundles two. A headless-only site installs it too:

```sh
npm install @zag-js/react @zag-js/core @zag-js/types @zag-js/carousel @zag-js/tabs @zag-js/clipboard
```

The package is ESM-only and supports React 19.

## Set up

Leave out `renderer` and `createPostkit` uses the headless views:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, technical } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, technical],
});
```

Wrap your app in `postkit.Provider` and pass `postkit.mdxComponents` to MDX,
as in the [Quick start](/docs/quick-start).

## Every part has a name

Every headless view stamps the component name on its root and a part name on
each part, along with its state:

```html
<aside
  data-postkit-component="Callout"
  data-postkit-part="root"
  data-tone="tip"
  data-size="md"
  data-variant="subtle"
>
  <span data-postkit-part="icon" aria-hidden="true">…</span>
  <div data-postkit-part="content">…</div>
</aside>
```

State follows the Ark UI conventions Chakra v3 uses, such as
`data-state="open"`, `data-current` and `data-tone`. The Chakra renderer emits
the same attributes, so selectors you write for one work for the other.

## Style it

Target parts with attribute selectors:

```css
[data-postkit-component='Callout'] [data-postkit-part='icon'] {
  color: var(--brand);
}
```

Or pass class names per part, which suits Tailwind and other utility CSS. They
are applied alongside the part names, so the two approaches mix. See
[Part styles](/docs/part-styles) for both.

## The optional stylesheet

Headless doesn't mean unstyled by force. `@postkit/react/styles.css` is a
small, optional baseline with a quiet, neutral look: structure, prose rhythm
and restrained monochrome. Every value in it is a `--postkit-*` custom
property, so you can retune it with [tokens](/docs/tokens) instead of
overriding rules.

```ts
import '@postkit/react/styles.css';
```

Load your own CSS after it, or leave it out and start from bare, named parts.

The stylesheet follows the reader's colour mode. Its custom properties get dark
values under `prefers-color-scheme: dark`, and under `.dark` and
`[data-theme="dark"]` for hosts that switch themes with a class, such as
next-themes. A light-only site that ignores the reader's setting should mark
its root `class="light"` or `data-theme="light"`, so the components stay light
too. CodeBlock, CodeGroup and Terminal keep their dark surface in both modes.

Set any of these on `:root`, or on any element for a subtree. The stylesheet
declares them with zero specificity, so your own rule wins whatever the order.
Give each colour you change a dark value too.

| Group           | Custom properties                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Colour          | `--postkit-color-bg`, `-fg`, `-fg-muted`, `-surface`, `-surface-emphasized`, `-border`, `-border-muted`, `-border-strong`, `-accent`, `-accent-fg`, `-focus-ring`, `-highlight`, `-letterbox`, `-on-letterbox`; `--postkit-color-scheme` (`light` or `dark`) |
| Tone            | `--postkit-tone-{note,tip,important,warning,caution}` and `--postkit-tone-{tone}-surface`                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Chart           | `--postkit-chart-1` to `--postkit-chart-4`, for series without an authored colour                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Code surface    | `--postkit-code-bg`, `-header-bg`, `-selected`, `-border`, `-fg`, `-fg-muted`, `-success`, `-focus-ring`                                                                                                                                                     |
| Type            | `--postkit-font-body` and `--postkit-font-heading` (unset: the host's), `--postkit-font-mono`; `--postkit-text-{xs,sm,md,lg,xl,2xl,3xl,4xl}`; `--postkit-leading`, `--postkit-leading-tight`; `--postkit-weight-{medium,semibold,bold}`                      |
| Space and shape | `--postkit-space-{1,2,3,4,5,6,8}`, `--postkit-space-flow` (between blocks); `--postkit-radius-{sm,md,lg,xl,full}`; `--postkit-border-width`, `--postkit-rule-width`; `--postkit-focus-width`, `--postkit-focus-offset`; `--postkit-duration`                 |
| Footnotes       | `--postkit-footnote-{accent,marker-color,marker-size,number-color,number-size,text-size,text-color,rule,rule-width,target-bg}`, `--postkit-sidenote-width`, `--postkit-sidenote-gap`                                                                         |

```css
:root {
  --postkit-font-heading: 'Fraunces', serif;
  --postkit-color-accent: #3b2f8f;
}
.dark {
  --postkit-color-accent: #c9c1ff;
}
```

Inside a component, `--postkit-inset` (the padding for its size) and
`--postkit-tone` and `--postkit-tone-surface` (its resolved tone) are set on
the root, so your part rules can reuse them.

Every rule in the stylesheet is wrapped in `:where()`, so a single class or
attribute selector beats it. To keep it below your own cascade layers, import
it into one: `@import '@postkit/react/styles.css' layer(postkit);`. It scopes
each component with CSS `@scope`, so a Callout's rules never reach a component
inside it; browsers without `@scope` show the semantic markup unstyled.

## Behaviour

Interactive behaviour, such as carousel paging, code copy, tabs and
consent-to-embed, is written once as a headless hook and shared by every
renderer. Postkit's Chakra views use the same hooks, and both pass the same
behaviour tests.

In 0.3.0 every built-in component has a headless view, the interactive ones
included: `Tabs`, `CodeBlock`, `CodeGroup`, `Carousel`, `Poll`, `LinkPreview`,
`NewsletterSignup`, `ShareActions` and `SocialPost` read their behaviour from
`useTabs`, `useCarousel`, `useCodeCopy`, `useEmbedConsent`, `usePoll`,
`useNewsletterSignup` and `useShareActions`. None is `chakra-only`.
Footnotes use `useFootnotes` for their placement (see
[Footnotes](/docs/footnotes)).

The hooks are exported, so you can build your own interactive views on the
same behaviour. Each returns the state plus prop getters to spread onto your
elements:

```tsx
import { useTabs } from '@postkit/react';

function Install() {
  const api = useTabs({ values: ['npm', 'pnpm'] });
  return (
    <div {...api.getRootProps()}>
      <div {...api.getListProps()} aria-label="Install">
        <button {...api.getTriggerProps({ value: 'npm' })}>npm</button>
        <button {...api.getTriggerProps({ value: 'pnpm' })}>pnpm</button>
      </div>
      <div {...api.getContentProps({ value: 'npm' })}>npm install</div>
      <div {...api.getContentProps({ value: 'pnpm' })}>pnpm add</div>
    </div>
  );
}
```

The headless package has no provider of its own, so views that need host
configuration take it as props: `LinkPreview` and `SocialPost` take
`resolveLink` and `socialServices`, `NewsletterSignup` takes `newsletter`,
`ShareActions` takes `socialServices` and `onShare`, and `Poll` takes
`onVote`.

## Chakra

Source: /docs/chakra

`@postkit/chakra` is the Chakra UI renderer for React. It has a Chakra-backed
view for every built-in component, supplies the Markdown and MDX tooling, and
ships Postkit's optional visual preset. The framework adapters (Next.js, React
Router, TanStack Router, and Astro) render through it.

`@postkit/chakra` was named `@postkit/react` before 0.3.0. From 0.3.0,
[`@postkit/react`](/docs/headless) is the headless renderer, and the Chakra
components moved here unchanged: replace the dependency and update your
imports.

```sh
npm install @postkit/chakra @chakra-ui/react @emotion/react react react-dom
```

It needs React 19 and Chakra UI `>=3.29.0 <4`.

## Use it with createPostkit

Pass `chakra` as the renderer to [`createPostkit`](/docs/create-postkit):

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { chakra } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article, media],
  defaults: { Callout: { variant: 'plain' } },
});
```

`postkit.Provider` then takes `PostkitProvider`'s props, described below.
Theme-variant `defaults` (`variant`, `size`, `tone`…) are written into the
recipes' `defaultVariants`, and other defaults become view defaults (see
[Defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots)).

## Entry points

| Import                                    | Contains                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@postkit/chakra`                         | Components, `chakra`, `PostkitProvider`, the MDX map, recipes, theme |
| `@postkit/chakra/theme`                   | `createPostkitSystem`, `createPostkitTheme`, `postkitDefaultTheme`   |
| `@postkit/chakra/remark`                  | `createPostkitRemarkPlugins` and the Remark transform                |
| `@postkit/chakra/document`                | `DocumentRenderer` and the `@postkit/core` parsers and serializers   |
| `@postkit/chakra/component-manifest.json` | The generated component manifest                                     |

The focused entry points keep React components out of theme libraries and
build-only Markdown tooling.

## The provider

Render articles beneath `PostkitProvider`. It supplies Chakra context and the
site-wide Postkit configuration:

- `system`: the site's Chakra system. Its tokens, recipes, and global styles
  are preserved.
- `preset`: optional visual defaults beneath the system. Pass
  `postkitDefaultTheme` for Postkit's standalone appearance.
- `theme`: scoped overrides from `createPostkitTheme`, applied last.
- `codeBlock` and `codeBlockAdapter`: code-block defaults and an optional
  syntax highlighter (see [MDX](/docs/mdx)).
- `resolver` or `resolvers`, with `defaultResolver`: runtime link resolution
  for `LinkPreview` (see [Link previews](/docs/link-previews)).
- `figures` and `figureLabel`: `figures="numbered"` numbers Figure, Video and
  Device ("Fig. 1", "Fig. 2") in reading order.

```tsx
import { PostkitProvider } from '@postkit/chakra';

<PostkitProvider system={siteSystem}>{article}</PostkitProvider>;
```

## Styling modes

- Host-native: pass the site's `system` and omit `preset`. The host's Chakra
  recipes control presentation.
- Standalone preset: pass `preset={postkitDefaultTheme}` for Postkit's complete
  visual treatment, including its dark CodeBlock, CodeGroup, and Terminal
  palettes.
- Scoped customization: add `theme={createPostkitTheme(...)}` to either mode.

[Tokens](/docs/tokens) covers the layering, and [Part styles](/docs/part-styles)
covers per-part overrides.

## Recipes and views

Each component's look is a Chakra slot recipe, exported as
`postkit<Name>Recipe` (such as `postkitCalloutRecipe`) with its part names as
`postkit<Name>Slots` (Aside shares Callout's), and registered under the recipe key
`postkit<Name>`. The parts carry the same `data-postkit-*` anatomy attributes
as the [headless](/docs/headless) views, so selectors written for one work
for the other.

To replace a component's render, build a view with `postkitChakraView`, which
takes the definition, the recipe and a render function (see
[Views](/docs/views)). To start from Postkit's own view instead, eject it with
`npx postkit eject <name> --renderer chakra` (see [Eject](/docs/eject)).

## Presentation props

Portable components share compact presentation controls:

- `size`: `sm`, `md`, or `lg`
- `variant`: `outline`, `subtle`, or `plain`

Site-wide visual decisions belong in the Chakra system or Postkit theme rather
than repeated content props. The [component catalog](/components) lists every
component with live previews, its props, and its directive syntax.

## Rendering documents

To render a portable document (from HTML, Markdown, MDX, or JSON) rather than
compiled MDX, use `DocumentRenderer` from `@postkit/chakra/document`. See
[Portable documents and feeds](/docs/portable-documents).

## Email

Source: /docs/email

Your posts already have callouts, figures and footnotes. `@postkit/email`
turns the same file into an email that looks right in Gmail, Outlook and Apple
Mail, so the newsletter is never a second draft.

## Render a post

`renderEmail` takes an authored post and returns email-safe HTML, a plain-text
version and any warnings:

```ts
// scripts/send-issue.ts
import { renderEmail } from '@postkit/email';

const { html, text, warnings } = await renderEmail(post.body, {
  format: 'mdx',
  baseUrl: 'https://example.com',
  definitions: postkit.definitions, // your createPostkit() set
});

await newsletter.send({ subject: post.title, html, text });
```

Hand `html` and `text` to any provider. Postkit never sends anything itself.

## Options

| Option          | Description                                                                        |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `format`        | `'mdx'`, `'markdown'` or `'document'` (a `@postkit/core` document).                |
| `theme`         | Optional Chakra Email theme. Defaults to the light Postkit email theme.            |
| `baseUrl`       | Resolves relative links and images, such as `'https://example.com'`.               |
| `components`    | Optional overrides, keyed like your MDX map: components by name, prose by element. |
| `wrapper`       | Optional layout component for the header, footer and unsubscribe link.             |
| `definitions`   | The components the post may use. Defaults to every built-in.                       |
| `url`           | The post on your site, where `link` fallbacks point.                               |
| `audiences`     | The audiences this email is for, for `AudienceBoundary`.                           |
| `newsletterUrl` | Where a `NewsletterSignup` would link.                                             |
| `pretty`        | Indents the HTML, for review.                                                      |

`format` defaults to `'markdown'` for a string and `'document'` for an object.
It resolves to `{ html, text, warnings }`. To use only part of a post, as a
digest does, call `parseEmailSource` first, pick the nodes you want, and pass
the result with `format: 'document'`.

## How it works

`renderEmail` parses the post with Postkit's Remark preset and directive
validation, as your site does, then `@postkit/core`'s safe MDX parser. Invalid props fail as they
do on the site; unknown components, MDX code (`import`, `{expressions}`) and
dangling footnotes become warnings instead. It maps each component to its
email view, or to the component's declared fallback, and renders the result
with Chakra Email's `render()`. The plain-text part comes from the same
document, so it makes the same decisions as the HTML.

It doesn't depend on a framework. Email is rendered in scripts, scheduled jobs
and queue workers as often as in a page, so `renderEmail` lives in
`@postkit/email`, not in the framework adapters.

Email always renders in the light theme. Email clients apply their own dark
mode.

## What's supported

| Components                       | Status    | In the inbox                                 |
| -------------------------------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Callout · Aside · CallToAction   | Supported | Table layout, inline styles, your tones      |
| Figure · Audio · Video           | Supported | Image with caption; media as a linked poster |
| KeyTakeaway · PullQuote · Steps  | Supported | Boxed summary, ruled quote, numbered rows    |
| Stat · ProductCard · LinkPreview | Supported | LinkPreview as a static card, never an embed |
| Footnote · Footnotes             | Supported | Numbered notes at the end, no links          |
| Everything else                  | Fallback  | Declared per component: text, link or omit   |

The status on each component page is computed from what `@postkit/email`
exports, so it can't drift out of date. Footnotes always render as end notes
with superscript numbers and no links, because in-message anchors are
unreliable across clients. The plain-text part marks them `[1]`.

## Fallbacks

Interactive components can't run in an inbox. Each one declares what to do
instead, so a newsletter never shows a broken widget:

| Fallback | What readers see                                    | Used by                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `text`   | The content as plain, readable text, code and links | AppearsOn, AudienceBoundary, AuthorCard, CardGrid, Carousel, Chart, CodeBlock, CodeGroup, Comparison, Device, Diff, Disclosure, FileCard, FileTree, Gallery, RelatedContent, SeriesNavigation, SponsorBlock, Tabs, Terminal |
| `link`   | A short line linking to it on the web               | Poll (to your post), SocialPost (to the post itself)                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `omit`   | Nothing; the block is skipped                       | ShareActions, NewsletterSignup                                                                                                                                                                                              |

Your own components declare one the same way, with `email: { fallback: 'text' }`
in `definePostkitComponent`. A component of your own with no email view and
no fallback renders as text. When a fallback applies, or a component is
unknown, `renderEmail` adds an entry to `warnings`, with a `code` such as
`email-fallback` or `unknown-component`, a `message`, and the component and
position when there is one. It never throws on content your site renders.

To give your own component an email view, or replace a built-in one, pass it
in `components`. A component with a view is never a fallback.

## Views and the provider

`renderEmail` is built from parts you can use directly. The package exports:

- Views: `Aside`, `Audio`, `Callout`, `CallToAction`, `Figure`, `Footnote`,
  `Footnotes`, `KeyTakeaway`, `LinkPreview`, `ProductCard`, `PullQuote`,
  `Stat`, `Steps` and `Video`, and `postkitEmailViews`, the map of all of
  them that the manifest's `support.email` is computed from.
- `PostkitEmailProvider`, which applies `postkitEmailTheme` (light, with
  literal `tone.*` and `tint.*` colours) and accepts Chakra Email theme
  overrides on top, such as your own tones.
- `createPostkitEmailMdxComponents()` and `postkitEmailMdxComponents`, the MDX
  map of the views, for email builds that compile trusted MDX.
- `parseEmailSource`, the parsing step of `renderEmail`.

```tsx
import { render } from '@chakra-email/core';
import { Callout, CallToAction, PostkitEmailProvider } from '@postkit/email';

const html = await render(
  <PostkitEmailProvider>
    <Callout title="Before you publish" tone="warning">
      Review the destination and audience.
    </Callout>
    <CallToAction
      title="Read the field guide"
      primaryLabel="Read now"
      primaryHref="https://example.com/guide"
    />
  </PostkitEmailProvider>,
);
```

Audio and Video never emit native media elements, because major email clients
don't support them consistently.

## Next.js

Source: /docs/nextjs

`@postkit/next` layers `next/link` over `@postkit/chakra`. Internal links stay
native to the Next.js router, while external URLs, protocol links, hashes,
downloads, and explicit non-default targets remain normal anchors.

```sh
npm install @postkit/next @postkit/chakra @chakra-ui/react @emotion/react react react-dom
```

It supports Next.js 15 and 16 with React 19 and the matching `@postkit/chakra`
release.

## Register the MDX components

Create the native MDX component map in `mdx-components.tsx`:

```tsx
// mdx-components.tsx
import { createPostkitNextComponents } from '@postkit/next';
import type { MDXComponents } from 'mdx/types';

export function useMDXComponents(components: MDXComponents): MDXComponents {
  return createPostkitNextComponents({ components });
}
```

The returned value is an MDX component map. Components supplied through
`options.components` override Postkit defaults, so site components take final
precedence:

```tsx
export function useMDXComponents(): MDXComponents {
  return createPostkitNextComponents({
    components: {
      h2: ArticleHeading,
    },
  });
}
```

Each Postkit component in the map loads the first time a page renders it, so
a page only downloads the components its content uses. Next.js waits for them
on the server, so the HTML is complete, and the browser keeps that HTML in
place until the component has loaded, so nothing shifts. For a synchronous
render such as `renderToStaticMarkup`, pass the eager views:
`createPostkitNextComponents({ components: postkitChakraViews })`.

## Mount the provider

Mount `PostkitProvider` in the application's provider tree:

```tsx
import { PostkitProvider, postkitDefaultTheme } from '@postkit/chakra';

export function Providers({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <PostkitProvider preset={postkitDefaultTheme}>{children}</PostkitProvider>
  );
}
```

The preset is optional; omit it when the host Chakra recipes should provide the
visual policy. The application owns its Chakra system, page layout, content
loader, and Next.js image configuration.

## Customize links

Next-specific link props can be supplied globally or derived for each
destination:

```tsx
export function useMDXComponents(): MDXComponents {
  return createPostkitNextComponents({
    link: {
      linkProps: { prefetch: false },
      mapLinkProps: ({ href }) => ({
        scroll: !href.startsWith('/reference/'),
      }),
    },
  });
}
```

## Remote MDX

The same map works with runtimes such as `next-mdx-remote`. Compile with
Postkit's Remark plugins so plain Markdown directives become components:

```tsx
import { createPostkitRemarkPlugins } from '@postkit/chakra/remark';
import { createPostkitNextComponents } from '@postkit/next';
import { MDXRemote } from 'next-mdx-remote';
import { serialize } from 'next-mdx-remote/serialize';

const components = createPostkitNextComponents();

const source = await serialize(markdown, {
  mdxOptions: { remarkPlugins: createPostkitRemarkPlugins() },
});

<MDXRemote {...source} components={components} />;
```

The package README and the checked Next.js example in the repository's
`examples/next` directory contain the complete adapter API.

## React Router

Source: /docs/react-router

`@postkit/react-router` routes internal destinations through React Router and
leaves external URLs, protocol links, hashes, downloads, and explicit
non-default targets as native anchors.

```sh
npm install @postkit/react-router @postkit/chakra @chakra-ui/react @emotion/react react react-dom react-router
```

It supports React Router 7 with React 19 and the matching `@postkit/chakra`
release.

## Create the component map

```tsx
import { createPostkitReactRouterComponents } from '@postkit/react-router';

export const mdxComponents = createPostkitReactRouterComponents();
```

Render the article beneath both the application router and `PostkitProvider`:

```tsx
import { PostkitProvider, postkitDefaultTheme } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { BrowserRouter } from 'react-router';

export function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <PostkitProvider preset={postkitDefaultTheme}>
        <Article components={mdxComponents} />
      </PostkitProvider>
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}
```

The application owns route definitions, data loading, and the outer page
layout. The preset is optional; omit it when the host Chakra recipes should
provide the visual policy.

## Customize components and links

Site components take final precedence:

```tsx
export const mdxComponents = createPostkitReactRouterComponents({
  components: {
    h2: ArticleHeading,
  },
});
```

Router-specific link props can be supplied globally or derived for each
destination:

```tsx
export const mdxComponents = createPostkitReactRouterComponents({
  link: {
    linkProps: { prefetch: 'intent' },
    mapLinkProps: ({ href }) => ({
      preventScrollReset: href.startsWith('?'),
    }),
  },
});
```

If React Router reports missing context, move the rendered article beneath the
router provider. A checked example lives in the repository's
`examples/react-router` directory.

## TanStack Router

Source: /docs/tanstack-router

`@postkit/tanstack-router` converts internal Markdown destinations into router
links and keeps external URLs, protocol links, hashes, downloads, and explicit
non-default targets as native anchors.

```sh
npm install @postkit/tanstack-router @postkit/chakra @tanstack/react-router @chakra-ui/react @emotion/react react react-dom
```

It supports TanStack Router `>=1.120 <2` with React 19 and the matching
`@postkit/chakra` release.

## Create the component map

```tsx
import { createPostkitTanStackRouterComponents } from '@postkit/tanstack-router';

export const mdxComponents = createPostkitTanStackRouterComponents();
```

Render the article beneath the application's TanStack Router provider and
`PostkitProvider`. The application owns its generated route tree, data loading,
and page layout. `PostkitProvider` is host-native by default; pass
`preset={postkitDefaultTheme}` only when Postkit's standalone visual treatment
is wanted.

## Recover typed routes

Plain Markdown stores destinations as strings. Resolve those strings into the
application's generated route tree at the adapter boundary:

```tsx
export const mdxComponents = createPostkitTanStackRouterComponents({
  link: {
    linkProps: { preload: 'intent' },
    mapLinkProps: ({ href }) => {
      const article = /^\/articles\/([^/]+)$/.exec(href);

      return article
        ? {
            to: '/articles/$slug',
            params: { slug: article[1] },
          }
        : {};
    },
  },
});
```

The link mapper can return route-specific `to`, `params`, `search`, mask, and
preload props.

## Customize components

```tsx
export const mdxComponents = createPostkitTanStackRouterComponents({
  components: {
    h2: ArticleHeading,
  },
});
```

If router context is missing, move the article beneath the router provider. If
a generated route rejects a portable string, translate it in `mapLinkProps`. A
checked example lives in the repository's `examples/tanstack-router` directory.

## Astro

Source: /docs/astro

`@postkit/astro` renders Postkit declarations through Astro MDX, provides
Chakra context for every isolated React rendering boundary, and hydrates only
components that require a React runtime.

## Install

```sh
npm install @postkit/astro @postkit/chakra
npx astro add react mdx
npm install @astrojs/markdown-remark
```

It supports Astro `>=6.4 <8`.

Add the Postkit integration and its unified Markdown processor:

```ts
// astro.config.ts
import mdx from '@astrojs/mdx';
import react from '@astrojs/react';
import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config';
import { createPostkitAstroMdxOptions, postkitAstro } from '@postkit/astro';

export default defineConfig({
  integrations: [postkitAstro(), react(), mdx(createPostkitAstroMdxOptions())],
});
```

`createPostkitAstroMdxOptions()` selects Astro's unified processor because
Postkit's base Markdown lifecycle uses Remark plugins. Additional Remark
plugins belong in the Postkit preset's `before` or `after` lists, while Rehype
configuration can be passed alongside it.

## Use a custom Chakra system

`postkitAstro()` uses Chakra's host-native `defaultSystem` unless the site
provides a module that default-exports its own `SystemContext`:

```ts
postkitAstro({
  chakraSystem: './src/styles/postkit-system.ts',
});
```

Opt into Postkit's standalone preset from that module when desired:

```ts
import { createPostkitSystem, postkitDefaultTheme } from '@postkit/chakra';

export default createPostkitSystem({ preset: postkitDefaultTheme });
```

The relative path resolves from the Astro project root and is imported by both
the server renderer and hydrated islands. This avoids trying to serialize a
Chakra system through Astro island props.

## Render MDX

Pass the component map to imported MDX or to content collections:

```astro
---
import { render } from 'astro:content';
import { postkitAstroComponents } from '@postkit/astro/components';

const { Content } = await render(Astro.props.entry);
---

<Content components={postkitAstroComponents} />
```

Site components take final precedence:

```ts
import { createPostkitAstroComponents } from '@postkit/astro/components';

export const articleComponents = createPostkitAstroComponents({
  h2: ArticleHeading,
  Callout,
});
```

Use Postkit's JSX declarations in Astro MDX. Reserve `::postkit-*{...}`
directives for plain Markdown pipelines.

## Hydration policy

Audio and Video use native browser controls, while AppearsOn, Figure, and the
current Chart renderer are static, so Astro emits them without a client
runtime. Disclosure also works natively without hydration. Carousel, CodeBlock,
CodeGroup, LinkPreview, NewsletterSignup, Poll, ShareActions, SocialPost, and
Tabs use `client:visible` and hydrate only when they approach the viewport.

Poll selections are local unless the host supplies persistence. Host callbacks
such as `onVote` belong inside a hydrated React wrapper; functions cannot be
serialized as props across an Astro island boundary.

The package README and the repository's `examples/astro` directory, which is
built and inspected in CI, contain the complete API.

## createPostkit

Source: /docs/create-postkit

`createPostkit` configures everything a host needs from the set of components
it actually uses: the provider, the MDX map, the directive plugins and the
manifest.

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, technical, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';
import { chakra } from '@postkit/chakra'; // omit for headless views
import NextLink from 'next/link';

import { showcaseDefinition, Showcase } from './components/showcase';
import { CommuneFigure } from './components/figure';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article, technical, media],
  exclude: ['Poll'],
  components: [{ definition: showcaseDefinition, view: Showcase }],
  defaults: { Callout: { variant: 'plain' } },
  overrides: {
    Figure: { view: CommuneFigure },
  },
  link: NextLink,
});
```

## Options

| Option       | Description                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `renderer`   | The renderer that supplies the views. Pass `chakra` from `@postkit/chakra` for the Chakra views. Omit it for the headless views.                                                                          |
| `kits`       | The [kits](/docs/kits) to enable, such as `[article, technical]` from `@postkit/react/kits`.                                                                                                              |
| `exclude`    | Component names to leave out of the enabled kits, such as `['Poll']`.                                                                                                                                     |
| `components` | Your own components and third-party ones, as `{ definition, view }` pairs. See [New components](/docs/new-components).                                                                                    |
| `defaults`   | Site-wide prop defaults, keyed by component name. See [Defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots).                                                                                                     |
| `overrides`  | Per-component slot and view overrides, keyed by component name.                                                                                                                                           |
| `link`       | The link component for internal links, such as Next.js `Link`. The framework adapters set it for you.                                                                                                     |
| `remark`     | Options for the Remark preset, such as `{ postkit: { strict: false } }` or `{ postkit: { footnotes: { defaults } } }` ([Footnotes](/docs/footnotes)). Directives always validate against the enabled set. |

### `defaults`

```ts
defaults: {
  Callout: { variant: 'plain' },
}
```

A prop an author writes always wins. With `@postkit/chakra`, theme-variant
props (`variant`, `size`, `tone`) are written into the recipe's
`defaultVariants`; other props become the view's defaults. The same object
works with the headless renderer.

`createPostkit` checks the object when it runs, and throws for a component
that isn't enabled, a prop it doesn't have, or a value the prop doesn't
allow.

### `overrides`

Each key is a component name. Each value can set:

| Key          | Rung | Description                                                                                                   |
| ------------ | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `classNames` | 3    | Class names per part, applied alongside the part names. See [Part styles](/docs/part-styles).                 |
| `slots`      | 5    | Components that replace single parts, keyed by part name. See [Defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots). |
| `view`       | 6    | A view that replaces the whole render. See [Views](/docs/views).                                              |

```ts
overrides: {
  Callout: {
    classNames: { root: 'rounded-sm border-l-4', title: 'font-display' },
    slots: { icon: InkMark },
  },
  Figure: { view: CommuneFigure },
}
```

Site `classNames` come first on each part, then an instance's own
`classNames`. A part name the component doesn't have throws, and the error
lists its parts. A view not built with `postkitView` or `postkitChakraView`
can't take `classNames` or `slots` overrides (see
[Defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots)).

`createPostkit` also throws when two kits or components define the same name
or directive, when `exclude` names something that isn't enabled, and when a
`components` entry repeats an enabled component. To replace a built-in
component's view, use `overrides.Name.view`.

## Returns

| Property                | Description                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `postkit.Provider`      | The renderer's provider (Chakra's `PostkitProvider` with `renderer: chakra`) with your defaults and overrides. Wrap your app in it once. |
| `postkit.mdxComponents` | Only the enabled components, plus prose. Pass it to your MDX runtime.                                                                    |
| `postkit.remarkPlugins` | The Remark plugins for MDX and Markdown. Directives validate against this set.                                                           |
| `postkit.manifest()`    | The `postkit.component-catalog` v2 [manifest](/docs/manifest) for this set.                                                              |
| `postkit.definitions`   | The enabled definitions that render with this renderer. Pass them to `renderEmail` ([Email](/docs/email)).                               |
| `postkit.renderer`      | The renderer in use.                                                                                                                     |

With `renderer: chakra`, `postkit.Provider` takes `PostkitProvider`'s props,
such as `system`, `preset` and `theme` (see [Chakra](/docs/chakra)). With
either renderer it also takes `figures="numbered"`, which numbers Figure,
Video and Device in reading order ("Fig. 1", "Fig. 2"). A Carousel or Gallery
counts as one figure whose items read "Fig. 3", "Fig. 3b", "Fig. 3c".
`figureLabel` changes "Fig.":

```tsx
<postkit.Provider figures="numbered" figureLabel="Figure">
  {children}
</postkit.Provider>
```

```tsx
// pages/_app.tsx
import type { AppProps } from 'next/app';
import { postkit } from '../lib/postkit';

export default function App({ Component, pageProps }: AppProps) {
  return (
    <postkit.Provider>
      <Component {...pageProps} />
    </postkit.Provider>
  );
}
```

## Framework adapters

`@postkit/next`, `@postkit/react-router` and `@postkit/tanstack-router` each
export a `createPostkit` preset. It takes the same options and returns the
same result, with `link` set to the framework's link; pass link options (or
your own component) as `link`. Image optimisation stays the host's job.

```ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/next';
import { article, technical, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';
import { chakra } from '@postkit/chakra';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article, technical, media],
  link: { linkProps: { prefetch: false } },
});
```

The low-level exports stay available: `createPostkitNextComponents()`,
`createPostkitReactRouterComponents()` and
`createPostkitTanStackRouterComponents()`, plus each adapter's link
(`createPostkitNextLink()` and so on).

## definePostkitComponent

Source: /docs/define-postkit-component

`definePostkitComponent` creates a component definition: the framework-free
contract for its props, its named parts and how it validates. Postkit's own
components and yours are defined the same way. It lives in
`@postkit/core/components`, so manifest tooling and editors can read
definitions without React.

```ts
// callout.definition.ts
import {
  definePostkitComponent,
  prop,
  presentation,
} from '@postkit/core/components';

export const calloutDefinition = definePostkitComponent({
  name: 'Callout',
  directive: 'postkit-callout',
  category: 'article-structure',
  description: 'A highlighted note, tip, warning, or caution.',
  children: 'mdx',
  runtime: 'static',
  stability: 'initial',
  props: {
    ...presentation,
    title: prop.string('An optional heading.'),
    tone: prop.enum(['note', 'tip', 'important', 'warning', 'caution'], {
      description: 'The semantic emphasis.',
      default: 'note',
      themeVariant: true,
      aliases: ['type'],
    }),
  },
  slots: ['root', 'icon', 'content', 'title', 'body'],
  keywords: ['note', 'admonition', 'alert'],
  example: {
    props: { tone: 'tip', title: 'Keep the content' },
    children: 'Change the renderer without changing the article.',
  },
});
```

## Fields

| Field         | Description                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`        | The PascalCase component name, used in MDX (`<Callout>`) and as the key in `defaults` and `overrides`.                                                            |
| `directive`   | The kebab-case Markdown directive name, such as `postkit-callout`.                                                                                                |
| `category`    | `article-structure`, `technical-content`, `media`, `discovery`, `engagement` or `publishing`. It groups the component in the manifest and in editors.             |
| `description` | A one-line description for the catalog and editors.                                                                                                               |
| `children`    | `'mdx'` when the component wraps authored content, or `'none'` (the default).                                                                                     |
| `runtime`     | `static` (the default), `native-controls`, `client` or `resolver`. `client` and `resolver` components hydrate in Astro.                                           |
| `stability`   | `initial` (the default), `experimental`, `stable` or `deprecated`. Editors can hide experimental components.                                                      |
| `props`       | The props, built with `presentation` and the `prop` builders.                                                                                                     |
| `slots`       | The anatomy: the named parts every renderer must emit. It must include `root`.                                                                                    |
| `keywords`    | Optional search terms for the catalog and editors.                                                                                                                |
| `example`     | Optional example props, and children for an `mdx` component, for the catalog and generated docs.                                                                  |
| `email`       | `{ fallback }`, where `fallback` is `'link'`, `'text'` or `'omit'`: what the email renderer does when it has no view for the component. See [Email](/docs/email). |

`definePostkitComponent` checks the definition when it runs and throws a
`TypeError` naming the component for anything it can't use: a name that isn't
PascalCase, a directive that isn't kebab-case, an unknown category, a missing
`root` slot, a prop not built with the builders, or example props the
definition doesn't declare. It returns the definition frozen, with the
defaults filled in and `themeVariants` listing the props marked as theme
variants.

## Props

`presentation` spreads in the shared `size` (`sm`, `md` or `lg`, default
`md`) and `variant` (`outline`, `subtle` or `plain`, default `subtle`) props.
The `prop` builders declare the rest:

| Builder                                  | Example                                                                            |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `prop.string(description, options?)`     | `prop.string('An optional heading.')`                                              |
| `prop.number(description, options?)`     | `prop.number('The start time, in seconds.', { default: 0 })`                       |
| `prop.boolean(description, options?)`    | `prop.boolean('Whether it starts open.', { default: false })`                      |
| `prop.enum(values, options)`             | `prop.enum(['note', 'tip'], { description, default: 'note', themeVariant: true })` |
| `prop.json<Type>(description, options?)` | `prop.json<Item[]>('The items, as a JSON array.', { required: true })`             |

A directive writes every value as a string: numbers and booleans are checked
and converted, a bare boolean attribute (`{open}`) means `true`, and a `json`
prop takes literal JSON, checked for syntax only. `prop.enum` takes its
description in the options, or a string in place of the options.

Options, for every builder:

- `required`: `true` makes the prop required. A directive without it fails
  validation, and views receive it as non-optional.
- `default`: the value when the author doesn't set one. It appears in the
  manifest and the props table, and views receive the prop as non-optional.
  An enum default must be one of its values.
- `aliases`: other names authors may use, such as Callout's `type` for
  `tone`. Directives, MDX props and the static serializer map an alias to
  the prop, and the prop wins when both are set (see
  [Validation](/docs/validation#aliases-and-warnings)).
- `recommended`: `{ reason, unless? }` for a prop authors should set. Leaving
  it out is a warning, never an error, in every mode. `unless` lists props
  that make it unnecessary, such as Video's `decorative`. A required prop
  can't also be recommended.

`prop.enum` and `prop.boolean` also take `themeVariant`: `true` makes the
prop a recipe variant automatically, and a site-wide default for it goes into
the recipe's `defaultVariants`.

## What it derives

From one definition, TypeScript derives the rest with no code generation:

| Derived                     | For Callout                                                                 |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Prop types for views        | `PostkitPropsOf<typeof calloutDefinition>`                                  |
| Prop types for authors      | `PostkitAuthoredPropsOf<typeof calloutDefinition>`                          |
| Slot union                  | `PostkitSlotOf<typeof calloutDefinition>`                                   |
| Variant union               | `PostkitThemeVariantOf<typeof calloutDefinition>`                           |
| Recipe key                  | `PostkitRecipeKeyOf<typeof calloutDefinition>`, which is `'postkitCallout'` |
| MDX map entry and directive | Registered when the component is enabled                                    |

`PostkitPropsOf` is what a view receives, so a prop with a `default` is never
optional. `PostkitAuthoredPropsOf` is what an author writes, where only
`required` props are required. All of these types come from
`@postkit/core/components`.

What TypeScript can't express is generated or computed from the definitions:
the [manifest](/docs/manifest) JSON, the Astro wrappers and the renderer
support matrix.

## Views

A view reads the definition. `postkitView` (headless) and `postkitChakraView`
(Chakra, with a recipe) give the render function typed `props` and a
`part(name)` helper that applies each part's attributes, class names and
styles, and both swap in slot overrides:

```tsx
import { postkitCalloutMarks, postkitView } from '@postkit/react';

export const Callout = postkitView(calloutDefinition, ({ props, part }) => (
  <aside {...part('root')}>
    <span {...part('icon')} aria-hidden="true">
      {postkitCalloutMarks[props.tone]}
    </span>
    <div {...part('content')}>
      {props.title && <p {...part('title')}>{props.title}</p>}
      <div {...part('body')}>{props.children}</div>
    </div>
  </aside>
));
```

See [Views](/docs/views) for writing one, and
[New components](/docs/new-components) for scaffolding a definition and view
together.

## Manifest

Source: /docs/manifest

The manifest is the machine-readable catalog of components: each one's
name, directive, props, parts and renderer support. Editors such as Prismark
read it to offer writers the components a site renders, and agents and other
tooling read it instead of importing a renderer.

Its id is `postkit.component-catalog`. Version 2 ships with 0.3.0.

## Get the manifest

For the set your site enabled, call `manifest()` on your Postkit:

```ts
import { postkit } from './lib/postkit';

const manifest = postkit.manifest();
```

Or write it from the terminal, for editors that read it from your repo. The
[CLI](/docs/cli#postkit-manifest) loads your config and prints the same JSON,
or writes it to `--out`:

```sh
npx postkit manifest --out public/postkit-manifest.json
```

Either way, the manifest describes exactly the components you enabled, your
own included, not everything installed.

`@postkit/chakra/component-manifest.json` is the manifest of every built-in
component. A package that ships components of its own can publish one too,
written with `createPostkitComponentManifest` from `@postkit/core/components`,
and `mergePostkitComponentManifests` combines several into one.

## What v2 adds

Version 2 keeps every v1 field and adds:

| Field          | Level     | Description                                                                                      |
| -------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `package`      | Component | The package that defines it.                                                                     |
| `kit`          | Component | The [kit](/docs/kits) it belongs to.                                                             |
| `stability`    | Component | `initial`, `experimental`, `stable` or `deprecated`. Editors can hide experimental components.   |
| `support`      | Component | Which renderers support it, computed from what each package exports rather than written by hand. |
| `slots`        | Component | The anatomy: the named parts every renderer emits.                                               |
| `variants`     | Component | The props that are theme variants.                                                               |
| `default`      | Prop      | The value when the author doesn't set one.                                                       |
| `themeVariant` | Prop      | Whether the prop is a recipe variant.                                                            |
| `aliases`      | Prop      | Other names authors may use for the prop, such as Callout's `type`. Only when it has some.       |
| `recommended`  | Prop      | `{ reason, unless? }` for a prop that warns when it's missing, such as Video's `captions`.       |

A v2 component entry, shortened to one prop:

```json
{
  "name": "Callout",
  "directive": "postkit-callout",
  "description": "A highlighted note, tip, warning, or caution.",
  "childMode": "mdx",
  "directiveRemarkPlugins": ["directives", "postkit"],
  "props": {
    "tone": {
      "kind": "enum",
      "values": ["note", "tip", "important", "warning", "caution"],
      "description": "The semantic emphasis of the aside.",
      "default": "note",
      "themeVariant": true,
      "aliases": ["type"]
    }
  },
  "slots": ["root", "icon", "content", "title", "body"],
  "variants": ["size", "variant", "tone"],
  "category": "Article structure",
  "kit": "article",
  "package": "@postkit/core",
  "keywords": [
    "callout",
    "article",
    "structure",
    "size",
    "variant",
    "title",
    "tone"
  ],
  "example": { "props": {}, "jsx": "…", "directive": "…" },
  "preview": { "kind": "live", "label": "Callout component preview" },
  "runtime": "static",
  "stability": "initial",
  "support": {
    "react": "supported",
    "headless": "supported",
    "chakra": "supported",
    "astro": "static",
    "email": "supported"
  }
}
```

`kit` is `null` and `package` is what you pass (or `null`) for your own
components. `components` is an object keyed by component name, alongside the
manifest's `id` (`postkit.component-catalog`), `version` (`2`) and
`declarationVersion`.

## Support

The `support` field is computed from what each renderer package exports:

| Field      | Values                                            | Meaning                                                                                            |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `react`    | `supported`, `not-supported`                      | v1's field: some React renderer has a view.                                                        |
| `headless` | `supported`, `chakra-only`, `not-supported`       | `@postkit/react`. `chakra-only` means only `@postkit/chakra` has a view; no built-in is, in 0.3.0. |
| `chakra`   | `supported`, `not-supported`                      | `@postkit/chakra`.                                                                                 |
| `astro`    | `static`, `hydrated`                              | Whether Astro hydrates it.                                                                         |
| `email`    | `supported`, `{ "fallback": … }`, `not-supported` | `@postkit/email`, or the definition's declared fallback: `text`, `link` or `omit`.                 |

`astro` is `hydrated` for `client` and `resolver` components, and `static`
otherwise.

A renderer the manifest's producer doesn't know is left out: a headless
site's `manifest()` has no `chakra` field, and `email` is there only when the
producer read `@postkit/email`'s views. `component-manifest.json` has it;
`@postkit/chakra`'s `postkitComponentCatalog` doesn't, since it doesn't depend
on `@postkit/email`, and neither does `postkit.manifest()`. To add it to a
manifest you write, pass
`renderers: { email: Object.keys(postkitEmailViews) }` to
`createPostkitComponentManifest`. A component is supported in email when
`@postkit/email` exports a view for its definition; otherwise `renderEmail`
applies the fallback the definition declares (`{ "fallback": "text" }`,
`"link"` or `"omit"`, see [Email](/docs/email)). Component pages show the
same data, so they can't drift from the packages.

## Version 1

v1 stays readable. `readPostkitComponentManifest` from
`@postkit/core/components` takes either version and returns v2, filling what
v1 never recorded with neutral values (no slots or variants, `package: null`,
the kit from the category, and no `email`, since v1's `not-defined` was a
placeholder). `isPostkitComponentManifestV2` and
`isPostkitComponentManifestV1` tell them apart, and
`mergePostkitComponentManifests` combines several:

```ts
import { readPostkitComponentManifest } from '@postkit/core/components';
import manifest from '@postkit/chakra/component-manifest.json';

const catalog = readPostkitComponentManifest(manifest);
```

A v1 component entry looks like this:

```json
{
  "name": "Callout",
  "directive": "postkit-callout",
  "description": "A highlighted note, tip, warning, or caution.",
  "childMode": "mdx",
  "directiveRemarkPlugins": ["directives", "postkit"],
  "props": {
    "tone": {
      "kind": "enum",
      "values": ["note", "tip", "important", "warning", "caution"],
      "description": "The semantic emphasis of the aside."
    }
  },
  "category": "Article structure",
  "runtime": "static",
  "stability": "initial",
  "support": { "react": "supported", "astro": "static", "email": "not-defined" }
}
```

The entry is shortened here: `props` also lists `size`, `variant` and `title`,
and each entry carries `keywords`, `example` and `preview`. The
`email: "not-defined"` value in v1 is a hand-written placeholder that v2
replaces with computed support.

## CLI

Source: /docs/cli

One small tool for the moments config isn't enough: turning on kits, taking a
component into your repo, keeping it current, and making your own.

The CLI is `@postkit/cli`, and its command is `postkit`. It depends only on
`@postkit/core` and file tooling, so it works with either renderer.

```sh
npm install --save-dev @postkit/cli
```

Once it's installed, `npx postkit` runs your project's copy. To try it without
installing, use the package name: `npx @postkit/cli eject figure`. A bare
`npx postkit` outside a project would look for a different, unscoped package.

## Commands

```sh
npx postkit --help
npx postkit eject --help
```

| Command            | What it does                                      | Example                    |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `postkit add`      | Turn on a kit or component and update your config | `npx postkit add media`    |
| `postkit eject`    | Copy a component's view into your repo to own it  | `npx postkit eject figure` |
| `postkit diff`     | See what changed upstream since you ejected       | `npx postkit diff figure`  |
| `postkit new`      | Scaffold a component of your own                  | `npx postkit new showcase` |
| `postkit manifest` | Write the catalog for editors like Prismark       | `npx postkit manifest`     |

Names work in any case: `figure`, `Figure`, `code-block` and `CodeBlock` all
work. `npx postkit --version` prints the installed version.

Every command takes `--config <file>`. An error you can fix, such as a
component that doesn't exist or a file that's already there, prints as one
line and exits with 1.

## Your config

Every command that needs your `createPostkit` config finds it the same way:

1. `--config <file>`, if you pass it.
2. `postkit.config.ts` (or `.mts`, `.js`, `.mjs`) in the current directory,
   then in the project root (the nearest `package.json`). It exports your
   `createPostkit` result as `default` or `postkit`:

   ```ts
   // postkit.config.ts
   export { postkit as default } from './lib/postkit';
   ```

3. Otherwise, the one file in your project that calls `createPostkit(`. If
   there's more than one, the CLI stops and asks for `--config`.

`add` and `eject` edit the file that calls `createPostkit({ … })`, following
`postkit.config.ts` to it. They only change what they can read with
certainty: a single call with an object literal, array literals for `kits`,
`components` and `exclude`, and an object literal for `overrides`. Anything
else, such as kits built in a function or options spread from another
object, is left alone, and the CLI prints the exact lines to add instead.

## postkit add

```sh
npx postkit add media
npx postkit add poll
```

```text
✓ lib/postkit.ts   kits += media
✓ lib/postkit.ts   components += Poll
```

A kit name (`article`, `technical`, `media`, `discovery`, `engagement`,
`publishing`) is imported from `@postkit/react/kits` and added to `kits`. A
built-in component whose kit is already on is taken out of `exclude`;
otherwise its definition (from `@postkit/core/components`) and your renderer's
view (from `@postkit/react` or `@postkit/chakra`) are imported and added to
`components`. A name that's neither a kit nor a built-in component stops with
a hint to run `postkit new` instead.

| Flag        | Default    | Meaning                               |
| ----------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `--config`  | discovered | The config file                       |
| `--dry-run` | `false`    | Print the change as a diff, unwritten |

## postkit eject

Ejecting copies the view (and its recipe, for Chakra) into your repo. The
definition stays upstream, so your posts, validation and editor support don't
fork.

```sh
npx postkit eject figure --renderer chakra --to libs/postkit
```

```text
✓ libs/postkit/figure/figure.recipe.ts
✓ libs/postkit/figure/figure.tsx
✓ .postkit-eject.json   Figure @ @postkit/chakra 0.3.0
✓ lib/postkit.ts   overrides.Figure.view → ../libs/postkit/figure/figure

Still bound to Figure's definition from @postkit/core/components.
It imports @postkit/chakra, @postkit/core, @postkit/react; keep them in your dependencies.
Chakra applies the recipe registered as postkitFigure first: register the ejected recipe in your theme to use your edits (see /docs/eject).
Run `postkit diff figure` after upgrading @postkit/chakra.
```

The folder is `<--to>/<component>/`. With `--renderer headless`, you get the
view and its CSS instead of a recipe. Without `--force`, eject stops if a file
it would write already exists.

| Flag            | Default       | Meaning                               |
| --------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `--renderer`    | from config   | `headless` or `chakra`                |
| `--to`          | `src/postkit` | Where the component's folder goes     |
| `--dry-run`     | `false`       | Show the files and config change only |
| `--force`       | `false`       | Overwrite files that already exist    |
| `--no-register` | registers     | Leave your config alone               |

"From config" means `chakra` when your config passes `renderer: chakra` from
`@postkit/chakra`, and `headless` when it has no renderer. See
[Eject](/docs/eject) for when to use it.

## postkit diff

After an upgrade, see exactly what upstream changed in the views you own, and
decide what to bring across.

```sh
npx postkit diff figure
```

```text
Figure (chakra) in libs/postkit/figure: @postkit/chakra 0.3.0 → 0.3.2
--- a/figure.tsx	@postkit/chakra@0.3.0
+++ b/figure.tsx	@postkit/chakra@0.3.2
@@ -59,7 +59,7 @@
           alt={alt}
           htmlWidth={postkitImageDimension(props.width)}
           htmlHeight={postkitImageDimension(props.height)}
-          loading={props.loading}
+          loading={props.priority ? 'eager' : props.loading}
           decoding="async"
           sizes={props.sizes}
           srcSet={props.srcSet}

1 file changed upstream. Your copy wasn't changed.
Your edits: figure.recipe.ts.
```

Without a name, it checks every component in `.postkit-eject.json`. When
nothing changed upstream, it prints `No upstream changes.`

| Flag          | Meaning                                                         |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--accept`    | Record the installed version as your new base, once you're done |
| `--exit-code` | Exit with 1 when upstream changed, for CI                       |

## postkit new

Scaffold a component with its definition, headless view and styles. It gets a
Markdown directive, validation and a manifest entry for free.

```sh
npx postkit new showcase
```

```text
✓ src/postkit/showcase/showcase.definition.ts
✓ src/postkit/showcase/showcase.tsx
✓ src/postkit/showcase/showcase.css

Register it with createPostkit({ components }) in lib/postkit.ts:

import { Showcase } from '../src/postkit/showcase/showcase';
import { showcaseDefinition } from '../src/postkit/showcase/showcase.definition';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  // …your renderer and kits
  components: [{ definition: showcaseDefinition, view: Showcase }],
});

Use it as <Showcase /> in MDX or :::postkit-showcase in Markdown.
Import showcase.css from your global stylesheet for the headless view.
```

With `--chakra` it also writes `showcase.recipe.ts` and `showcase.chakra.tsx`,
and the registration uses the Chakra view. With `--spec` it writes a spec per
view (`showcase.spec.tsx`, and `showcase.chakra.spec.tsx` with `--chakra`).

| Flag                 | Default             | Meaning                                      |
| -------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `--to`               | `src/postkit`       | Where the component's folder goes            |
| `--chakra`           | `false`             | Also a Chakra view and slot recipe           |
| `--spec`             | `false`             | A spec per view (Vitest)                     |
| `--category`         | `article-structure` | The catalog category                         |
| `--directive`        | `postkit-<name>`    | The Markdown directive                       |
| `--description`      |                     | The one line editors and the catalog show    |
| `--import-extension` | `none`              | `js` for Node's `nodenext` module resolution |
| `--dry-run`          | `false`             | List the files without writing them          |
| `--force`            | `false`             | Overwrite files that already exist           |

In an Nx workspace, `nx g @postkit/nx:component showcase` writes the same files
from the same templates. See [New components](/docs/new-components).

## postkit manifest

```sh
npx postkit manifest --out public/postkit-manifest.json
```

Loads your config (TypeScript and TSX work) and writes the v2 manifest of
exactly the components it enables, yours included, to stdout or `--out`. It's
the same JSON as `postkit.manifest()`, for editors like Prismark. With
`--out`, it confirms on stderr:

```text
✓ public/postkit-manifest.json   from lib/postkit.ts
```

`manifest` finds the config like the other commands (see
[Your config](#your-config)). The module must export the `createPostkit`
result as `default` or `postkit`, or as its only export with a `manifest()`
method.

## API reference

Source: /docs/api-reference

Postkit generates its API reference from the public exports of every published
package.

- [Browse the TypeScript API reference](/api/)
- [Download the TypeDoc JSON model](/api/postkit-api.json)
- [Download the component manifest](https://unpkg.com/@postkit/chakra/component-manifest.json)

Use the guides for task-oriented setup and the API reference for exact
signatures, return types, and exported interfaces. The component manifest is
the smaller authoring contract for editors and component browsers; the TypeDoc
model describes the complete TypeScript library surface.

## Compatibility and environments

Source: /docs/compatibility

Postkit packages are ESM-only, publish TypeScript declarations, and emit
ES2022 JavaScript. The host application's framework and build tool must support
those package conventions.

## Framework matrix

| Integration     | Supported range | Rendering notes                                                            |
| --------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| React           | React 19        | Chakra-backed components render on the server and client                   |
| Chakra UI       | `>=3.29.0 <4`   | The host may provide a `SystemContext`; Postkit layers its recipes over it |
| Shiki           | `^4.3.1`        | Optional lazy highlighting through `@postkit/shiki`                        |
| Next.js         | `>=15 <17`      | Uses the native MDX component map and `next/link`                          |
| React Router    | `>=7 <8`        | The article must render beneath a router provider                          |
| TanStack Router | `>=1.120 <2`    | Portable URLs can be mapped into generated route types                     |
| Astro           | `>=6.4 <8`      | Uses matching React, MDX, and Markdown integrations                        |

The package manifests are authoritative for exact peer dependency ranges.

## Runtime matrix

| Capability                     | Environment                                                  |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Document parsing/serialization | Any ES2022 ESM runtime; React is not required                |
| React rendering                | Server rendering or a browser-capable React application      |
| Static Astro components        | Build/server render with no component hydration              |
| Interactive Astro components   | `client:visible` islands                                     |
| Native audio and video         | Browser-native controls; no Postkit client runtime           |
| Unfurling                      | Server, build process, or trusted editor with Web Fetch APIs |
| Plain Markdown transforms      | Node/build tooling using Unified and Remark                  |
| Shiki syntax highlighting      | Lazy client runtime beneath `PostkitProvider`                |
| Email rendering                | Build or server rendering with Chakra Email primitives       |

Carousel, CodeBlock, CodeGroup, LinkPreview, NewsletterSignup, Poll, ShareActions,
SocialPost, and Tabs hydrate as visible Astro islands. Other current Astro
bridges render statically; Audio, Video, and Disclosure retain native browser
controls.

## Repository tooling

The repository's CI and release workflow use Node.js 24 and npm. Consumers do
not need Node.js 24 merely to render browser components, but their selected
framework, build tool, and server runtime must satisfy their own requirements
and support Postkit's ES2022 ESM output.

## Stability

Postkit is pre-1.0. Public APIs are typed and clean-consumer tested, but minor
releases may refine the component contract. Pin related `@postkit/*` packages
to the same release version and review the changelog before upgrading.

## Security and trust boundaries

Source: /docs/security

Postkit separates portable authored content from trusted application
infrastructure. Treat every URL, metadata response, saved snapshot, and
Markdown document as untrusted input.

## Remote resolution

Run `@postkit/unfurl` in a server, build process, or trusted editor. Provider
credentials must never enter the rendered document or browser bundle.

Provider adapters send the authored URL to a configured metadata service.
Custom resolvers that fetch origins directly must protect against server-side
request forgery:

- Accept only intended protocols
- Block private, loopback, link-local, and cloud metadata destinations
- Revalidate every redirect
- Enforce timeouts and response-size limits
- Restrict content types and parse depth
- Cache normalized results under an application-owned policy

## Embeds

Resolvers may retain provider markup as `embed.rawHtml`. Postkit's React
renderer never injects that field. A host that chooses to render it owns HTML
sanitization, iframe isolation, content security policy, consent, and provider
allowlisting.

Validated iframe and media URLs are still third-party resources. Apply the
host's `sandbox`, `allow`, referrer, privacy, and consent policies.

## Authored content

Plain Markdown directives accept allowlisted literal values and do not execute
authored JavaScript. MDX is executable JavaScript and should only be compiled
from authors trusted at that level, or processed inside an appropriately
isolated publishing pipeline.

React escapes text values, but host-supplied components and callbacks remain
host code. Validate URLs and structured JSON before passing them into custom
renderers.

## Reporting

Report suspected vulnerabilities privately through the repository's
[GitHub security page](https://github.com/postkit-org/postkit-js/security).
Do not include secrets or publish a proof of concept in a public issue.

## Troubleshooting

Source: /docs/troubleshooting

## Components render with only host styling

This is the default. Postkit inherits the host Chakra system and does not apply
its visual preset automatically. Pass `preset={postkitDefaultTheme}` for the
standalone appearance, register Postkit slot recipes in the host system, or use
`theme={createPostkitTheme(...)}` for deliberate scoped overrides. The article
must still render beneath `PostkitProvider` so Chakra context is available.
CodeBlock, CodeGroup, and Terminal retain semantic structural styling in this
mode, but their opinionated dark palettes belong only to the standalone preset.

## Internal links reload the page

Use the framework adapter rather than the base React MDX map. Render the article
beneath the router provider and verify that the destination is considered an
internal URL by the adapter.

## A plain Markdown directive is ignored

Enable Postkit's Remark plugins and use the `postkit-` directive name. Use JSX
instead of directive brace syntax inside MDX files.

## Astro hydration fails

Confirm that the React and MDX integrations are enabled and that a custom Chakra
system is exported from a module addressable by both server rendering and
hydrated islands.

## Link previews do not resolve

Run the resolver on a server or at build time. Check the provider configuration,
URL policy, response contract, and cache independently from the rendering
component.

When reporting an issue, include the Postkit package version, framework and
runtime versions, a minimal content sample, and whether the failure occurs at
build time, server rendering, hydration, or client interaction.

## Package: @postkit/unfurl

Source: https://github.com/postkit-org/postkit-js/tree/main/packages/unfurl

# `@postkit/unfurl`

Provider-neutral link metadata resolution for Postkit renderers and publishing
pipelines. The package runs in a server, build, or trusted editor process; it
does not ship API keys or origin-fetching logic to article readers.

## When to use it

Use `@postkit/unfurl` when a server or build process needs to turn an arbitrary
URL into a stable `ResolvedLinkPreview` for link cards, media, oEmbed, or social
post rendering. Applications that already produce this normalized contract can
use Postkit renderers without this package.

## Install

```sh
npm install @postkit/unfurl
```

The package is ESM-only, has no browser runtime requirement, and includes
TypeScript declarations.

## Quick start

OpenGraphs is the default provider when a resolver registry is created:

```ts
import {
  createIframelyResolver,
  createLinkResolverRegistry,
  createOpenGraphsResolver,
} from '@postkit/unfurl';

export const linkResolver = createLinkResolverRegistry({
  resolvers: [
    createOpenGraphsResolver({
      apiKey: process.env.OPENGRAPHS_API_KEY,
    }),
    createIframelyResolver({
      apiKey: process.env.IFRAMELY_API_KEY!,
    }),
  ],
  fallbackProviders: ['iframely'],
});

const metadata = await linkResolver.resolve('https://example.com/article');
const alternate = await linkResolver.resolve('https://vimeo.com/123', {
  provider: 'iframely',
});
```

Adapters are included for:

- OpenGraphs (`https://unfurl.opengraphs.com/v1/resolve`)
- Iframely
- Embedly
- Microlink

Every adapter normalizes its response into `ResolvedLinkPreview`. Provider
markup is retained as `embed.rawHtml` for hosts with their own sanitization
boundary, but Postkit's React component only uses validated HTTP(S) media and
iframe source URLs.

Fallback providers are opt-in. This prevents an outage or malformed response
from unexpectedly consuming credits with another service.

## Public API

The package exports:

- Provider adapters for OpenGraphs, Iframely, Embedly, and Microlink
- `createLinkResolverRegistry`
- `createCallbackResolver`
- Normalized link, media, embed, and social metadata types
- Versioned social-post snapshot helpers and guards

Resolvers accept an abort signal, provider selection, preferred embed
dimensions, and a force-refresh option.

## OpenGraphs response contract

Postkit sends a `GET` request to
`https://unfurl.opengraphs.com/v1/resolve` with `url`, and optionally
`maxwidth`, `maxheight`, and `force` query parameters. If `apiKey` is
configured, it sends `Authorization: Bearer <apiKey>`.

The canonical version-one envelope is exported as `OpenGraphsResponse`.
`resolver` identifies OpenGraphs; `data.provider` identifies the upstream
content or oEmbed provider:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "requestId": "1d6275d3-c72a-4215-ad9d-1a7b809a9bf5",
  "resolver": {
    "id": "opengraphs",
    "name": "OpenGraphs",
    "url": "https://opengraphs.com/"
  },
  "data": {
    "canonicalUrl": "https://example.com/posts/launch",
    "title": "Launch notes",
    "description": "What shipped and why.",
    "siteName": "Example",
    "author": "Ada Lovelace",
    "authorUrl": "https://example.com/authors/ada",
    "favicon": "https://example.com/favicon.ico",
    "images": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/launch.jpg",
        "alt": "The launch",
        "type": "image/jpeg",
        "width": 1200,
        "height": 630
      }
    ],
    "audio": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/launch.mp3",
        "type": "audio/mpeg",
        "durationSeconds": 185
      }
    ],
    "video": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/launch.mp4",
        "type": "video/mp4",
        "width": 1280,
        "height": 720,
        "poster": "https://example.com/launch-poster.jpg"
      }
    ],
    "embed": {
      "type": "video",
      "src": "https://player.example.com/launch",
      "rawHtml": null,
      "thumbnail": {
        "url": "https://example.com/launch-poster.jpg",
        "alt": "Launch video",
        "type": "image/jpeg",
        "width": 1280,
        "height": 720
      },
      "width": 1280,
      "height": 720,
      "aspectRatio": 1.7777777778,
      "title": "Launch video"
    },
    "provider": {
      "id": "example",
      "name": "Example",
      "url": "https://example.com/"
    },
    "social": {
      "service": "bluesky",
      "url": "https://bsky.app/profile/ada.example/post/abc",
      "author": {
        "name": "Ada Lovelace",
        "handle": "@ada.example",
        "url": "https://bsky.app/profile/ada.example",
        "avatar": "https://cdn.example.com/ada.jpg"
      },
      "text": "The launch is live.",
      "publishedAt": "2026-07-26T14:30:00Z",
      "images": [
        {
          "url": "https://cdn.example.com/social-launch.jpg",
          "alt": "Launch announcement",
          "type": null,
          "width": 1200,
          "height": 675
        }
      ],
      "video": [],
      "metrics": {
        "replies": 4,
        "reposts": 12,
        "likes": 80,
        "shares": 2
      },
      "quotedPost": {
        "service": "bluesky",
        "url": "https://bsky.app/profile/example.com/post/xyz",
        "author": {
          "name": "Example",
          "handle": "@example.com",
          "url": null,
          "avatar": null
        },
        "text": "Original announcement.",
        "publishedAt": null,
        "images": [],
        "video": [],
        "metrics": null
      }
    }
  },
  "cache": {
    "strategy": "use",
    "result": "hit",
    "fetchedAt": "2026-07-26T14:31:00Z",
    "expiresAt": "2026-07-26T15:31:00Z",
    "maxAgeSeconds": 3600
  },
  "resolution": {
    "kind": "metadata",
    "requestedMode": "auto",
    "requestedUrl": "https://example.com/posts/launch",
    "requester": "GENERIC",
    "upstreamError": null
  }
}
```

The normalized `ResolvedLinkPreview` preserves the request ID, cache strategy
and result, resolution context, resolver identity, and upstream provider. An
embed thumbnail becomes `embed.thumbnail`; `durationSeconds` remains explicit;
zero-valued metrics and `maxAgeSeconds: 0` are retained. Unsupported schema
versions or a non-OpenGraphs resolver identity are rejected.

The adapter still accepts the legacy flat response without the `data`
envelope. For compatibility it recognizes these aliases:

- `canonical` or `url` for `canonicalUrl`; `site` for `siteName`;
  `author_url` for `authorUrl`; and `logo` for `favicon`.
- A single `image`, `audio`, or `video` item instead of an array. Media URLs
  may use either `url` or `src`; legacy `duration` maps to
  `durationSeconds`.
- `oembed` for `embed`, `html` for `embed.rawHtml`, and `url` for
  `embed.src`. Raw HTML is retained but never injected by Postkit.
- `social.network` for `social.service`, `postUrl` for `social.url`,
  `content` for `social.text`, `published_at` for `publishedAt`,
